speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before motions are proceeded with I should like to rise to a question of privilege. Last night's ten o'clock news bulletin of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation contained an item which reflected upon members of the House of Commons. The news broadcast stated that Canada's largest war appropriation bill, amounting to $3,890,000,000, was given its first, second and third readings within a few minutes during yesterday's session-I believe "ten minutes" was the actual expression used. Such a statement, without an explanatory background, might readily lead Canadian listeners to conclude that insufficient consideration had been given by the House of Commons to this important measure. Actually no legislation of like character in Canadian parliamentary history had been the subject of as close scrutiny and inquiry, or had been as long and thoroughly debated as the resolution upon which this bill was founded.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext: I am glad that government members seem to be satisfied that we have made a good job of scrutiny. It is true that the formal readings of the bill required only a few minutes of the time of the house, but in justice to hon. members in this chamber I think it should be asserted that 44 out of the 117 sitting days of this session have been spent in debating that resolution. I rise to this point of privilege in order that there may be no possible misunderstanding on the part of the public in the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
I have prepared a memorandum which helps to emphasize what the leader of the opposition has just said.
On February 26 the Minister of Finance moved that the house go into committee to consider the war appropriation bill. On March 3 the Minister of Finance presented a table showing a break-down of the various estimates. Then the resolution was considered in committee on May 13, 14, 18, 21, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 and 31; June 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14,15, 16, 17, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 28, 29 and 30; July 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 21 and again yesterday. As my hon. friend has said, it has been considered during 44 sittings, lasting over a period of nine weeks. I believe that fact makes it quite clear that, as my hon. friend stated, there has been no financial measure in the history of this parliament which has received the amount of consideration-careful consideration-and full discussion that this particular measure has received.
May I point out at this time wherein I believe the error made in the news broadcast arose. As the house is aware, money bills are preceded by resolutions. I have said time and again to the Clerk of the House who, from my conversations with him, holds a similar view, and so states in his volume dealing with procedure in the house, that the resolution was never intended to be more than a notice to the house that a money bill was being brought down, and that it had been approved by His Excellency the Governor General. I have pointed out, and he agrees, that it was never intended that a lengthy debate should take place on the resolution stage of any financial measure. The resolution is intended to be in the nature of a warning to the house that a financial measure is to be considered. Certainly, until recently, this parliament has passed many such resolutions as a formal procedure. However we have begun to adopt the practice, one to which I have objected time and again, and to which I still object of proceeding to discuss at length on the resolution stage the main features of a bill. This session of parliament, or a very large part of it, has
been taken up in the discussion of the resolution in question. There was nothing further left to discuss on the bill itself that is why no discussion whatever was required when the bill was presented, and why there was no delay in passing its second and third readings. I hope these points will be made clear to the public, because they are in explanation of why the bill itself, which was based on a resolution, passed through the house as rapidly as it did. The whole subject matter was very fully discussed on the resolution stage.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has discussed the point in some detail, and I believe I might be justified in adding something further. In order that there may be no misunderstanding on the part of the public, and that we may not have the criticism which from time to time is offered to the effect that large sums of money are passed through parliament with what, to some, is regarded as inadequate consideration, may I add a word with respect to the civil estimates we are now considering. I believe hon. members will agree that the principles embodied in the estimates for civil expenditures and the subjects covered thereby were in most instances dealt with at length when we were discussing the war appropriation resolutions. I believe therefore it would not be in the interests of the country or of parliament that in the discussion of the civil estimates there should be any great measure of repetition.
True, there are some matters which do not come within the purview of the war appropriation, and to 'these we as the opposition intend to give the greatest care and scrutiny as they are presented. But I think it would be the wish of parliament and of the country that there should be no unnecessary repetition of discussion in a war time period. I make this statement as complementary to that which has been made by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. GRAYDON BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-CBC NEWS BROADCAST RESPECTING WAR APPROPRIATION BILL
speechtext:
Again I should like to thank the leader of the opposition for having directed the attention of the house and the country to a very important matter. I agree entirely with all that he has said. With respect to the ordinary estimates, they have been before 'the house from the moment the debate on the address was completed. They differ little in any particular from the ordinary estimates which have been voted year after year by this house during the last four years. They relate to the necessary business of government, hon. members have discussed similar items in previous sessions, perhaps not the exact amounts that are here, but the subjects that are indicated, and hon.

Toronto Shipbuilding Company
members know whether the items have changed in a significant way. Moreover, the government has sought to ascertain from the different parties any particular items in the estimates which any of their members feel should be brought forward for consideration before other estimates are taken up. In other words, if there are any estimates which hon. members who have given special study to 'the estimates feel should be considered before others, the government will try to meet the wishes of hon. members in that regard. But it is true that the war appropriation bill has dealt with practically all departments of government and there has been on that measure the fullest opportunity for discussion of practically everything bearing upon the various subjects which appear in the ordinary government estimates.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT IN RESPECT TO SUPPLIES FOR CANNING IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition
asked me to make a statement about the situation in the United States with regard to the supply of sugar in the United States for canning purposes.
Our latest advice from the United States is that all consumers may obtain a general allowance of 10 pounds per head for home canning and preserving. In addition, upon application to a local ration board, and completion of various declarations each applicant may be allowed additional sugar up to a maximum of fifteen pounds per head, thus providing for a maximum possible allowance of 25 pounds per head, as stated by the leader of the opposition.
While this plan has been announced, it is not clear as to just what will happen if a large number of people in the United States do in fact apply for the extra allowance. If the experience is similar to that in this country, the total amounts applied for will far exceed both the amount of sugar available, and the amount required to put up such fruit as is available.
The over-all international allocation of sugar is made by the combined food board, on which Canada is represented. Sugar consumption in the United States in 1942 was
10,610,000,000 pounds, compared with 900,000,000 pounds in Canada. This is an approximately equal per capita amount. Presumably the over-all international allocation will continue to maintain this balance, and ;ach country will have to make its own .ntemal allocation. The amount allocated to any one purpose within Canada-or in the United States-can only be decided in the light of all relevant circumstances, particularly the amount used for other related purposes, such as the amounts used for commercial jam making and fruit packing.
In spite of the anticipated reduction in the fruit crop this year, the amount of sugar allocated for home canning is the same as the amount used last year. There is no justification for an assumption that more sugar will be required. What has happened is that a far greater number of people will participate in the use of sugar for home canning this year-with a consequent reduction in the amounts which heretofore were used by some persons. This is what rationing does.

Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of fustice) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to bill No. 107, to amend the criminal code.
He said: I so move because, at this stage of the session, I do not think it would be appropriate to ask for a conference to discuss these amendments which have to do with sections 7 and 8 of the bill. Hon. members will remember the debate we had on those sections and how it was explained that they were introduced at the request of some of the attorneys general of the provinces who found difficulty in curbing as they would wish to do the evil of betting and bookmaking prevalent in their localities. Hon. members of the other house have come to the conclusion, from the situation in the country as they know it, that the amendments are unnecessary. They set up their opinion against the opinion of the attorneys general who are administering justice. I regret it. I should have preferred to
see the bill stand as passed by this house. But there will be other sittings of this house, and if in the meantime the opinions expressed by the attorneys general are persisted in from the result of their experience, I shall expect to have the honour at another session to come back before parliament with appropriate suggestions. In the meantime, one of the amendments consists in striking out the clause that has to do with advertising, printing and publishing material likely to assist or likely to be used in connection with bookmaking.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO BETTING, PREVIOUS OFFENCE CHARGED, ETC.-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Section 8?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes. They struck out section 8 entirely. Though it had been subjected to the proviso that it would not apply to bona fide newspapers, the section in the code as it stood before was found by some of these attorneys general, or their deputies, to be insufficient to prevent the issuing of these tipster sheets which are very frequently put out for the purpose of aiding in bookmaking. The other house has refused to accept section 8. As to section 7, they have taken out the words, "in such manner as to be likely to be used," so that the former paragraph as it stood will remain, with the words inserted, "or outfitted or equipped" and will so read as to define a common betting house as a place open, kept or use or outfitted or equipped for the purpose of facilitating or encouraging or assisting in the making of bets. They have taken out, after "outfitted or equipped", the words "in such manner as to be likely to be used." So that under the provision as it stands, with their amendment, the court will still have to find the subjective intention of the person doing the thing with which he is charged.
I regret that they took that attitude, but at this time I do not think it would be advisable to have a conference over the matter, and I think we may see whether, with the insertion of the words they have left in, it meets the situation complained about by these attorneys general or whether anything further will be necessary at some future time.

This gives me an opportunity to bring to the attention of the minister the multitude of complaints hon. members have received since the minister last had his estimates before the committee in connection with the war appropriation resolution, because of the fact that, despite the attempts which have been made to simplify the income tax forms, they still remain exceedingly complex. A storm of protest has risen across the country in regard to this matter. Frankly as a layman I am not able to suggest to the minister how the forms may be simplified further under the present system of taxation. It may be that the system is at fault, but I believe people have great difficulty in differentiating between the normal tax and the graduated tax; and when you have in addition the various exemptions and the compulsory savings feature, it becomes almost a Chinese puzzle to the average man across Canada. In earlier years, before the incidence of taxation became so severe, this matter was not perhaps so serious; but to-day, with the heavy incidence of taxation and so many more of our people being required to make out these forms the matter has become exceedingly important. Many people are not in a position to obtain the assistance of lawyers and accountants; they have enough taken off their cheques and out of their pay envelopes already, without going to any further expense to have someone

Supply-Revenue-Income Tax
show them how much they must pay the government. Perhaps that is putting the matter in a very simple way, but I believe that is the way most of the taxpayers of Canada would put it to the minister if they were in this chamber. The whole matter of the incidence of our income tax will have to be given serious consideration by the minister in the interval between this and the next session of parliament. No doubt before this the minister and his assistants have reached the conclusion, in view of the protests that have come from every corner of the country, that some simpler way must be found whereby the people may contribute to the war effort. I am speaking as one who knows very little about accountancy; there are not many experts in that line in this house, but I can say that unless there is some further adjustment of the incidence of this taxation and some simplification of the forms by which taxes are calculated, there will be grave dissatisfaction throughout the country.
At this stage of the session I am not going to discuss this point in detail, but in what I have said I believe I am reflecting the views of hundreds of thousands of taxpayers in Canada who are finding it increasingly difficult to make out these forms. Having in mind the experience of the average person, I have no doubt the minister will find that the inaccuracies and errors in the income tax returns which have been filed this year will amount to a staggering total, and I doubt if the department will ever be able to catch up with those errors and assess the proper taxation. When you make your forms so complex that the average man or woman is unable to understand them, you run into a heap of trouble, which I think the department should make every attempt to avoid.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister only in order to reflect an ever-growing sentiment in this country. It may be that the suggestions of those of us who are not able to say how these difficulties may be overcome will not be very helpful, but having regard to the broad coverage of our taxation system I am convinced that something must be done to bring about some simplification of it. It is of immediate and imperative necessity that the departments alter the scheme in order that the people of Canada may know how the amount was arrived at, in a simple fashion, and in a manner which will meet the needs of the average citizen.

First of all, may I compliment the leader of the opposition upon drawing this matter to the attention of the minister. In fact I might doubly compliment him
because, despite his being a lawyer, he wishes to simplify rather than complicate forms for the preparation of which most people have had to have legal assistance.
And I am not so sure the lawyers know much about them either.

Yes, I am inclined to believe that, especially when one hears around the corridors of the House of Commons that many members of parliament, including some lawyers, were stuck when it came to answering questions appearing on the income tax form. In these circumstances, I have wondered how the average citizen has fared.
Complaints have been made in connection with the collection of income tax from workers. Much has been said about absenteeism. I am not saying that this manner of collection has been the cause of absenteeism, but I do know it is creating a great deal of indignation among the workers. I am reliably informed-and if my information is not correct, the minister will deny it-that while a worker may be deducted on the basis of his regular earnings, in the event of his beginning to work overtime the deductions are made at the overtime rate. Many workers are reluctant to work overtime, because they say if they do so, and their rate of pay is increased from, we will say, $1 to $1.50 an hour, the income tax deduction is made at the rate of $1.50 an hour. If this practice is now in effect, a change should be made so that taxation will be taken off at the ordinary rate of wages. I am told this practice has caused much discontent, and it may be the cause of a certain amount of absenteeism. I join with the leader of the opposition in the recommendation he has made.

The leader of the opposition has spoken about the complicated nature of our tax structure. I must agree with him that it is complicated, and that very fact places a great burden upon my department when it attempts to produce forms which make due provision for the sections in the Income War Tax Act. I believe the officers of the Department of National Revenue deserve some credit for the manner in which they have drawn up forms which include all allowances and deductions for which provisions are made in the act. They have made every effort to produce as simple a form as possible, under the act as it stands to-day. In addition they have produced, for those who use the T-l form, a simplified table for computing the total normal and graduated taxes, and I believe it is of great assistance to taxpayers in working out their taxation.

Supply-Revenue-Income Tax
Of course it does not help them in computing their taxable income. That must be done by completing the form itself.
The question of taxation of workers for overtime is one which has been given serious consideration. It is receiving attention at the present time, and we are attempting to find out if any other method may be adopted for deducting the tax at the source from a man who in one week earns perhaps a considerably increased amount as a result of his overtime work. While it would not affect his total tax over the year, if we could make some arrangement whereby we would take an average tax from his earnings, it would prevent an over-deduotion being taken from one payment, and a refund being necessary at a later date.

I should like to press upon the minister the necessity of doing something in connection with what is considered to be an excessive tax on the workmen in the coal mines. The production of coal is an emergency operation, as indicated by the Prime Minister, and known by almost everyone in the country. Householders in cities are not able to get any assurance that they will get coal this winter to heat their houses and places of business. I would not say that in the county of Cumberland any workmen have deliberately stopped work because of this tax. But I will say there is not the incentive to continue to produce, or to exert themselves unduly. They do not feel the urge to work six full days a week, and overtime, to bring about the necessary production, because they feel they are unduly penalized on any earnings they may make over and above a certain amount. I must say I have a great deal of sympathy for them in that point of view. It is understood that miners should not be expected to work more than four days in the week. When they work five or six days a week, and the extra earnings are taxed at what they consider an exorbitant rate, all incentive is destroyed. I would urge upon 'the minister that he come to some decision in the matter as quickly as possible, and give some concession to the coal miners in order that they may work to the full limit of their capacity.

The matter now under review was thoroughly discussed with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. I understand that on the basis of previous representations the department has been considering some modification of deductions at the source. Would the minister care to make a statement in respect of that matter?

I am glad to be able to say that to-day we are having discussions with representatives of the miners from the maritime provinces. The two officials with me this morning have been at that conference, and will be returning to it as soon as possible. An attempt is being made to arrive at some method of deduction which will provide that an undue deduction will not be made from a man's pay when overtime is included.

Who are
sitting in on that conference? Are representatives of the workmen on it?

Yes, the labour union as
well as representatives of the Department of Labour and of the Department of National Revenue.

I am
pleased to hear the minister say a conference is taking place with representatives of the miners from the maritime provinces. But I do not understand why only miners from the maritimes are being consulted, when there are miners in other parts of Canada. Their organizations should be consulted too, inasmuch as union officials are being consulted in the matter.
I should like to associate myself with what has been said in connection with taking the tax at the source. I believe that is a cause of much dissatisfaction, especially the feature of it connected with overtime. As has been pointed out, when the deduction is made at the source it is taken at the higher rate of pay, a fact which leads to much misunderstanding. A few days ago, when this matter was discussed at some length under the estimates of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue pointed out that a man was not taxed more because he produced more, and that therefore this factor should not be the cause of absenteeism. I did not know this item was to be discussed this morning, or I would have brought my correspondence to the chamber with me; but I believe I am quite safe in saying that I have at least half a dozen letters from people in different parts of the country, one of them from the maritimes and another from British Columbia, complaining about this situation. The letter from British Columbia pointed out that the writer was penalized $3 more in taxation because he was working overtime. If he had not worked overtime he would have been $3 ahead. The minister may say that a mistake has been made in computing the tax; I do not know, because I have not gone into the case thoroughly. However, there is considerable dissatisfaction when the tax is deducted at the

Supply-Revenue-Income Tax
source. The minister has said that a conference is being held to see if this difficulty cannot be overcome. If something can be done it will be worthwhile. As things stand at present the men are dissatisfied, and I believe this is one of the principal causes of absenteeism, not only in the coal mines but in our munitions and shipbuilding plants. If it can be made clear that men will not be penalized because they work overtime, I think a good deal of the dissatisfaction will be eliminated.
I believe in overtime production, but there should be some overtime or production rate paid. I speak without having given very deep thought to the matter, but probably some arrangement could be worked out whereby regular time free of taxation could be paid for overtime, instead of paying time and a half and then deducting the tax. Generally speaking, I think that would be a satisfactory arrangement. I have associated with workers for thirty years and I feel quite sure that there is not one of these men who is not desirous of going back to work longer hours, sometimes under severe handicaps, in order to increase our war production. This applies equally to men working in the mines and in our munitions factories. But they do resent being taxed) on their overtime pay. If straight time for overtime was paid without deducting at the source, I think you could increase your production a great deal.

When I said that we were meeting representatives of the miners from the maritimes, I should have stated that we are meeting representatives of miners from all over Canada. If the hon. member for Bow River will let me have the details of the case in which the man was taxed on his overtime, I shall be glad to look into it.

I am informed that no overtime is paid to the girls and women who work extra hours in the income tax branch. I do not know whether this condition prevails all over Canada, but it does in my own constituency. After working all day girls are ordered back at night. It is true they are paid sixty cents for their dinner, but they receive no pay for the extra time they work. I do not think they are getting a fair deal by being treated in this way. They should receive extra pay for the extra work they do. I should like to know the grounds upon which the government bases its decision that they should not be paid.

Overtime is not paid to
clerical workers in the civil service who are required to work extra hours. In war time it is necessary in some departments to work beyond
the hours that are customary in peace time. At the present time we have a heavy rush of work in the income tax branch. Our establishment has been increased, but the difficulty is to get qualified people to fill the positions as rapidly as we should like. There are times when the staffs are required to work overtime, but, as I say, throughout the civil service as a whole no overtime pay is granted to those who work extra hours.

If they belonged to a trade union they would quickly have overtime pay, probably time and a half. I cannot understand upon what basis you can ask these people to come back and work overtime and not pay them. It is not fair that they should have to work hard all day and then come back night after night and receive no extra pay. What hours are worked here in Ottawa?

The hours of the Ottawa office are from 8.15 a.m. to 5.15 p.m. We have a very loyal staff and have had no complaints from them when they are called upon to work overtime. They realize that in war time there are extra demands, and they have willingly accepted the situation as it exists.

Are we to infer from the minister's remarks that in these discussions about overtime pay andi taxation he was dealing only with priority industries, such as mining? Does he intend to work out a policy of income taxation for miners only?
It is not a change in policy; it is working out a change in the methods of deduction. It will not affect the rate of taxation at all.

It is not the intention of the government to work out some system under which miners can work overtime, without giving the same consideration to iron and steel workers, fuel wood producers, pulpwood producers and other workers in similar industries?
We are exploring it now with the mining industry. If we come to some arrangement, we will try it out and if it works satisfactorily we will see if it can be extended to other industries.

To-day there is a great need for increased fuel wood production, yet men in this industry are discontinuing their daily work in the middle of the afternoon rather than continuing and having their extra earnings taken up by the income tax. I urge upon the minister that he give consideration to this matter, not only from the point of view of the miners but from the point of
Supply-Revenue

Income Tax

view of the fuel wood producers. I believe that this is now a priority industry, similar to the coal mining industry. This system of deduction interferes drastically with other forest production, and during the last two years the effect has been quite serious. I think in connection with industries such as the iron and steel, coal and fuel wood and many others, a rate of taxation could be struck so that when a man has a total daily wage of $8 with overtime he will not have to pay so much on the last S3 that he considers he will be better off to stop work when he has earned $5. I hope the minister will make this applicable to other lines of production.

[Mr. Rowe.l
Mines and geology branch
121. Branch administration, $29,550.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two in connection with the mines and geology branch, in the hope of encouraging the minister to ask for more money perhaps next session in support of his staff of geologists, chemists and engineers. I recently visited the little plant on Booth street, where I met a number of the engineers and observed the handicaps under which they are working there. I am convinced the time has come when Canada should launch out under the Department of Mines and Resources and determine to develop from our own raw resources the thousand and one different products which we could produce. I am not going to mention any names, but the men I met down there were very bright men, some of them young men, and I just wondered whether our own geologists, engineers and chemists in the minister's department are being properly compensated. There is such a demand in the United States for men with their qualifications that I fear that if our own men are not properly compensated they may be taken away from us, and now is the time that this country requires men of the capacity of our geologists and engineers in the mines and geology branch. There have been marvellous developments of late that we are not profiting from in this country, and I am not sure that they are in the United States to the extent they should, but at all events they are on their way. I hope we will not let them get ahead of us in developing the natural resources of the country.
There are all sorts of developments for the use of the raw products with which this country abounds. Take the minister's own riding in northern Manitoba. There you have one of the finest stands of pulpwood. That would be a great place to develop a thousand and one industries in manufacturing the by-products from the production of pulp which to-day are largely lost. Take plexiglas, for instance, which is being developed in the United States, and many other such materials which we could be developing from our forest products and by-products. The field is unlimited.
I am not going to detain the committee,, but I am convinced that if the minister would ask for an appropriation that would enable him to equip his department with a building fitted with the most modem appliances, the department could achieve much more than it is possible for it to do to-day. Down on Booth street they have just a small hydrogenation plant, a very small affair. Why not:

Supply-Mines and Resources
install an adequate hydrogenation plant there? It would be well worth while when you consider the endless ramifications of fine products which could be developed from our raw resources. I for one will support the minister and the department in asking for an appropriation to erect any plant that is necessary for the purpose. It would have to be infinitely larger than that small building on Booth street. I will support any appropriation that is necessary to man the department with the ablest geologists, chemists and engineers obtainable. They are all good men down there now. One thing I like about the department is that they have such good men in it, but they are working there from motives of patriotism, because if they went to the United States they could command much larger salaries than they are receiving. They deserve credit for staying on the job and helping this country to develop its own natural resources. I am convinced that the Department of Mines and Resources has a golden opportunity to put this country on the map after the war in a thousand and one ways, and I hope that next session the minister will come forward with a request for a real appropriation to build and equip a modern building and give our engineers and geologists and chemists the opportunity of developing the innumerable products that are being developed by different processes elsewhere. I could enumerate forty different lines of production which could be made from our resources in Canada and which are not now being made.
I should like to see our own Canadian processes developed and ear-marked as being the product of Canadian brains. That is all I am going to say on the whole of these items. I am taking them all together and making this short statement covering them all. I hope that these good solid men in the minister's own department will be encouraged and supported to do something in a big way for Canada. But they will need equipment. They have not got it. Hydrogenation is perhaps the most modern process for the development of a thousand and one different lines. Let Canada take its place in the sun, and use its own resources and its own fine men in doing it.

I doubt if there is any member of the house who has given more thought to, or has endeavoured to inform himself more fully on, the natural resources of this country than the hon. member for Davenport, and I wish to express my thanks to him for the interest he has taken in the work of the department.
He is in a class by himself on that.

There is no doubt that not many Canadians, having regard to the total number of our population, have a full appreciation of the natural resources and the natural wealth of this country. I may say for the information of my hon. friend that in the war appropriation vote there was an estimate for an addition to the buildings of the mines branch. There will be spent on the building at present under construction about $230,000, and it is the best that all the thought we could bring to bear upon it could produce. In addition to that, about $150,000 will be spent for equipment in this particular work. That will add substantially to the facilities which the mines bureau have for carrying on their work.
But there is another part of my hon. friend's remarks to which I would like to allude. We have difficulty of course during the war in getting the personnel to carry on this work. That will be clear to the committee when I say that since the outbreak of war, from the department as a whole-this is as of last September, when these estimates were first put in draft form-202 employees had enlisted in the armed forces; of these, 32 came from the mines and geology branch. There were then on loan to other departments 34 employees, of whom 11 came from the mines and geology branch. So that since the outbreak of war our personnel in this branch, including men .who have enlisted and men who have been loaned, and these are among our best, have been reduced by 43. But that is due only to war conditions.
I certainly agree with my hon. friend that the public expenditure in this department could well be expanded. I have in mind particularly a much vaster programme than we have hitherto carried out in geological surveys and in mapping surveys of our country.
Once again I wish to express my appreciation of the interest which the hon. member for Davenport has taken in this matter.

Inasmuch as the Jasper national park, one of the largest and most beautiful parks in the world, lies within the boundaries of the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I wish to take this opportunity of saying a few words in regard to parks in general and in particular relation to the post-war period. During the present session, both within and without this house, we have had a considerable amount of discussion as to full employment being one of the major objectives in the post-war period. At this time I do not wish to enter into any debate on that issue; nevertheless I do suggest, as I did on a previous occasion, that I can agree with that objective provided we understand what we mean by full employment. If it means that we are going to use machines and our resources of power to the fullest extent possible, and man-power as little as possible, then I can agree; but if it means that we are to put the machines aside and allow them to rust by the roadside, as we did prior to the outbreak of war, and compel men to use picks and shovels and wheelbarrows to do the work we wish to have done, then of course I am entirely opposed to that understanding of full employment. I think Canadians need to learn not so much how to work as how to play. In the past I think far too much emphasis has been placed on the matter of work. Of course that raises a contentious subject, on which there could be much debate, and I am not going to impose my views on the committee now.

But it is a good thing
to have a job.

What the hon. gentleman
means is that it is a good thing to have an income, not necessarily a job. In the past we have suffered not so much from unemployment as "unempayment". We are all constantly endeavouring to get out of a job, and that includes my hon. friend and his associates. It has been the endeavour of man, ever since he has been upon this earth, to get out of all the nature-forced labour he possibly could in order that he might indulge in voluntary activities such as golf, if you like, or mountain climbing or swimming or a thousand and one other things which people do in their leisure time and in which they may expend more energy than in their working hours. I think we as members of parliament ought to be leading our people toward a new attitude in regard to life. The greatest philosopher who ever trod upon this earth said, "I have come that ye might have life and have it more abundantly." He did not say, "I have come that you might have jobs and work."
But he worked as a carpenter.

Quite true. That was necessary and dignified work; and I, believing in a new economic philosophy, agree that we must all be prepared to do our share of the necessary work that is involved in raising the standard of living to the point to which we wish it raised. In the past, however, people have not refused to do the necessary work, but governments and economists have allowed conditions to arise and to continue under which they have imposed their will upon the people and compelled them to do work which was not necessary or forced by nature. In this day and age, when we have the tremendous advantage of being citizens of the twentieth century, when we are the fortunate recipients of a great fund of knowledge, of science and invention, nature-forced labour could be reduced to the very minimum. I dare say that if in the post-war world we took advantage of all the machines and power production methods available, divided' up the necessary hours of work in an equitable fashion, and divided up the hours of spare time, we could possibly get along with a six-hour or a five-hour day, or even a four-hour day. I believe that is a desirable objective. Fundamentally that is the desire of each of us in the House of Commons, as well as those outside. We are endeavouring to free ourselves of nature-forced labour in order that we may have more spare time to indulge in voluntary activities.
That brings me to the point I have in mind in connection with our national parks. In my view our national parks should be one of the

means by which the people of Canada can use their leisure time with a maximum of benefit. I think we, as Canadians, shall have to put a good deal more emphasis on the cultural aspect of our lives than we have in the past. I certainly believe we have been putting far too much emphasis on the business and commercial aspects of our lives. True, there must always be a certain amount of business; but it seems to me that we make the objective-of our lives one of pure business and commercialism, and in doing so we fail to emphasize the cultural side. There is far too much talk about pure business matters in this parliament. I should like to hear much more discussion of our philosophical attitude toward life, and what we are getting out of it as a nation. I certainly believe that by reason of the way things have been conducted in the past we have encouraged our people to become a lot of muckraking money-grubbers, and that we ought to get away from that idea.
In the post-war period I should like to see a set of economic circumstances in which people collectively will not be obliged to spend their hours behind office desks, or at lathes, or in machine shops, any more than is absolutely essential in order to produce the standard of living we desire. What I believe the people of Canada need, and ought to have, is more time to play. I see no reason at all why, in the postwar period, every individual, regardless of his position in life, should not have at least two months holidays a year with pay.

Who will look after
that?
Machinery.
And who will make the machinery?

The machines will make the machinery. That is one aspect of our economy which most people who consider our economic problems entirely overlook. They seem to believe that we are still in the eighteenth century, and using a pick, shovel and wheelbarrow. The fact is that we are living in a modem, high-speed, mass-production era, in which production, so far as the limit is concerned, is greatly increased. I am not trying to suggest that we should have an era in which there is no work at all. Naturally there is always going to be a certain amount of nature-forced labour to do, and we should be prepared to do our share of it. If economic circumstances were such that we would not need to do any more than is absolutely essential, the working day could certainly be reduced far below what it is to-day, and the income increased proportionately.

An American naturalist named John Muir said a few years ago something which I believe is apropos of the matter we are now considering. This is what he said:
The tendency nowadays to wander in wildernesses is delightful to see. Thousands of tired, nerve-shaken, over-civilized people are beginning to find out that going to the mountains is going home; that wildness is a necessity and that mountain paths and reservations are useful not only as foundations of timber and irrigating rivers," but as fountains of life.
I think that is a valuable quotation. And, respecting our national parks, someone else has said this:
If the British industrialist, for instance, was to search the whole world where else could be found such delightful diversified holiday and health-building possibilities as exist in the national parks of western Canada? No matter what the park visitor's interest may be, he may enjoy himself to the utmost in some of this vast national park area of over twelve thousand square miles. He may canoe in the northern prairie parks following the canoe routes of the old-time traders, or he may camp, fish, swim and just loaf to his heart's content. In the mountain parks he may find more vigorous exercise in mountain climbing, exploring and hiking, or if his interest is in natural history in any of its branches, he may find wild animals and birds in abundance in many varieties.
These are the things to which we should be paying more attention in our national life; and were we to do so, we would be better for it. I resent the attitude of looking at our national parks as a basis for tourist trade. To my mind it smacks very much of commercialism. Our national parks and sites of natural beauty should be places where we could entertain our friends from abroad. We ought not to assess our parks in terms of dollars and cents to be drained from them, or as money we can get from our friends who come to visit us. If they wish to entertain us, by way of exchange for the manner in which we entertain them, well and good. Let us go to visit them, and let them entertain us by way of repayment for what we have done. But in my view we must get away from this idea of commercializing that which Should be part of our cultural life.
If I wished to elaborate on this subject there are many other statements I could make, but as hon. members are anxious to conclude the session I shall limit what I have to say. Certainly this is one aspect of our national life which we are overlooking too much. I trust when we reach the post-war period the Minister of Mines and Resources, and his colleagues, are not going to come along and say-if they happen still to be in their present position-that they cannot spend more money to hard-surface the roads of Jasper park or to extend tourist accommodation, because they

have not the money. That was the answer we got in pre-war days: "We have not the money." I believe the thought is thoroughly implanted in people's minds that if we can find five thousand million dollars a year for destructive purposes, certainly the same amount of money can be made available for constructive purposes and for enhancing the cultural life of our nation.
I trust that once we reach the post-war period we are not going to be confronted with the statement that no money is available to do these things. The only limitation imposed in war time is that of men and materials. In peace time those same men and materials will be available, no doubt in far greater quantities than they were during war time. As long as we have the physical essentials to put our parks in such condition that they will be most inviting to our friends from abroad, only physical limitations should be imposed and none other. I trust that the Minister of Mines and Resources will keep this in mind when he is considering the appropriations that are necessary for the development of our national parks.

In reply to the first question I would say that the Department of Justice has given a decision to the effect that as the Indians are British subjects they are liable to military service. That decision was sustained in a recent court action in the province of Quebec. I am not so familiar with the terms of the early treaties that were signed in the years past with the various bands of Indians but I do know that what I have stated is the legal position with regard to their liability to military service.
In regard to income tax, the Indians are not subject to income tax upon income they derive from their reserve, but if an Indian, for instance, passes through university and becomes a medical doctor or an engineer and practises his profession in an ordinary community outside the reserve, he is liable to income tax.

I think one matter to which the department should give consideration is the administration of the Soldier Settlement Act on the Indian reserves. As hon. members are aware, the Six Nations Indian reserve is the largest Indian reserve, in population, in the Dominion of Canada. It is in a purely agricultural country, one of the finest townships in the county of Brant. After the last war many of the Indians who had seen service took up soldier settlement lands on the reserve. The same disaster overtook them that overtook many other soldier settlers, and the result is that to-day the crown holds a mortgage or is the creditor on a number of those farms to an amount far in excess of their value. We were discussing the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act the other day, and here is one place where I think that act might have served a definite and useful purpose in securing the adjustment of those debts, but for some reason or other, whether it was because we did not interpret the act aright, or misinterpreted the Indian Act, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act did not apply to those lands. Many of these farms are to-day abandoned, because it would be impossible for a young man to take over one of these farms at the high prices that were paid for them in the boom years and with the large claim which the crown has against the property, the chattels and real estate. There may be a few who mastered their obligations, but not very many.
Soon Indian veterans will be returning from this war and something should be done to prevent what otherwise might be a terrible disillusionment for the veteran. As it is they will be reluctant to go into any soldier settlement scheme because of the results of

the administration of the Soldier Settlement Act on the Indian reserves. I am aware that the administration of Indian soldier settlement comes under a different department from ordinary soldier settlement, but I do feel that every effort should be made to get this thing cleared up as soon as possible. We shall probably have to rehabilitate our men when they return from the war, and let us not leave a bad taste in their mouths by failing to clear up the present situation. As the minister is no doubt aware, there has been considerable correspondence between the Indian Affairs branch at Ottawa and the hospitals association of British Columbia in regard to payment for the hospital care of Indians in that province. 2.	Hospitals throughout British Columbia refuse emphatically to discriminate on account of racial origin or religious differences, and insist that all patients should receive equal treatment, regardless of creed or race. They further point out that, contrary to the department's contention, the experience has been that often it costs more to care for Indians than ordinary patients, there being a greater need for isolation, pursuant to contagious and social diseases.
3.	The average basic cost for general ward patients is $3 per diem and that sum is the very minimum for which the institutions throughout British Columbia could attempt to give adequate care. This does not include extras, such as X-rays and so forth.
4.	The position taken by the department that the hospitalization of Indians is cheap does not hold. Experience is all to the contrary, and the hospitals wish to emphasize that it is their duty to protect and improve the health of the Indian, to a degree equal to that afforded other patients. A rate less than that hereinbefore stated simply means that the community at large is made responsible for a cost which is without a doubt an obligation of the department of Indian affairs, whose direct wards the Indians are.
5.	Hospital costs throughout the province have been examined closely by various organizations and the provincial government and all local contracts, including the workmen's compensation board, are at rates of not less than $3 per diem plus extras.
I invite the attention of the committee and of the minister to the next paragraph:
6.	Unless a revision is made all provincial hospitals will be compelled in the future to refuse the admission of Indian patients to their institutions. This may appear a harsh measure,

but as no redress has been forthcoming by the department they are left with no other alternative. Incidentally, every other department of the government of the dominion has recognized the factors hereinbefore enumerated and is paying fees akin to the basic rate outlined, and it is difficult to understand why recognition should be given on the one hand, even when it involves the care of enemy aliens such as the Japanese, and refused to Indians.
A statement, I understand, was forwarded to the minister by the secretary of the British Columbia Hospitals association, E. W. Neel. I am informed, although I cannot vouch for the accuracy of the assertion, that St. Joseph's hospital in Victoria has refused to admit Indian patients. I am informed of that but I do not know whether it is correct.
I have in my hand a statement from Creston, British Columbia, relative to the rates charged by the hospital at Creston for the care of Indian hospital patients, and the share of that bill that has been paid by the Indian department. There are a number of cases here with names given. I will quote a few of them:

A number of other cases are given. In May, 1942, the hospital cared for an Indian baby where there had to be an operation. The amount was $12.50. The department apparently refused to pay at all and consequently the cost had to be assumed by the local hospital at Creston.
I have discussed this matter with the department, and the department has assumed, in my opinion, an attitude that is not very enlightening. In a letter from the department to one of the hospitals in British Columbia the position was taken that if the hospitals insisted on the Indian department paying $3 a day, the department would have to reduce the cost by not sending cases to the hospital which 
formerly went there, or by moving cases from the hospital sooner than had been done previously.
I put these matters briefly before the committee because I think that this is a situation that should be dealt with. One of the stock answers made to the hospital administrators is that, for the purpose of paying these hospital charges, the Indian department has only such moneys as are granted to it by parliament. I submit that this is the time for the minister to ask parliament to grant sufficient money to decently care for the Indians who are given hospital treatment.
I now have under my hand the material for which I was looking. It is contained in a letter to myself from the secretary of the British Columbia Hospitals association, Mr. E. W. Neel, who says:
The department also states that Indians who are in a financial position to meet all or part of the cost of their hospitalization should be required to do so.
I have no objection to that.
This may apply to Indians who live outside the reservations and are no longer the direct wards of the federal government but for the hospitalization of reservation Indians who are the direct wards of the government and who form by far the major portion of Indian patients, the hospitals have no option but to look to the department for payment. In view, however, of the department's statement it would be interesting to know on how many occasions in British Columbia the department has recovered from reservation Indians the cost of their hospitalization or through the local Indian agent has notified a hospital that owing to an Indian's financial position, the hospital should look not to the department but to the patient for the payment of the hospital account.
Only two conclusions can be drawn from the attitude of the department. Either it does not want the same quality of hospitalization given to Indians that is given to other patients whether white or oriental, and this would seem to be indicated from the tone of a letter written by Mr. T. R. Mclnnis, secretary of the Indian branch at Ottawa on September 8 to the Nicola Valley hospital. In this letter Mr. Mclnnis stated_ that "if this branch is forced to pay these higher rates it will certainly not result in increased revenue for the institution concerned as we will have no alternative than to reduce the number of patients hospitalized. It means having to make your patients fit our funds, and we will either keep them out or hurry them out."
I think that is a terrible statement to be made by a civilized government in regard to the hospital care of its wards. This committee should insist that the Indian branch pay the hospitals in various parts of the country for the care of these wards of the government at the rates which are paid by organizations such as sick benefit associations, workmen's compensation boards and so on. Let it be noted that any additional charge which is not

paid by the government must be assumed by the citizens of the municipality concerned, and I believe this government has more facilities at its disposal for raising the necessary revenue than are available to the municipalities with which I am acquainted in the province of British Columbia. I have in my hand a copy of the Glace Bay Gazette of May 13, 1943, which carries a news item under the date line of Ottawa, May 12. The headline, in fairly bold type, is, "Better Health Plan for Indian Race is Forecast." It is dated Ottawa; I imagine it must apply to Canada, though from the information I have placed on record so far one would not gather that fact. The article states:
Lo, the poor Indian, who has dreamed away the years, will be transformed into a vigorous builder of a new and greater Canada if official hopes are realized.
Well, I do not know just what official hopes they would like realized, but I trust it is the official hopes of the Indian Affairs branch.
Indian affairs medical officers to-day told the story of a vast experiment in human welfare.
It must have been an experiment which they did not try.
If it succeeds-and the preliminary results make scientists' eyes sparkle-120,000 Canadian Indians will have better health. In addition- and just as important-their outlook on life probably will be changed for the better.
Before we can get a changed outlook on life on the part of the Indians I believe we will have to get a changed outlook on life on
the part of the Indian Affairs branch.
From one report, based on extensive studies and written in the light of most modern scientific knowledge, come the following:
What I have read was just newspaper talk,
I guess; this quotation is from the hopeful officials in Ottawa:
"It is not unlikely that many characteristics, such as shiftlessness, indolence, improvidence and inertia

Inertia is not confined only to the Indians.
-so commonly regarded as hereditary traits in the Indian race, may, at the root, be really the manifestation of malnutrition."
Well, whatever the cause, I hope this newspaper article is correct and that it foreshadows a different policy on the part of the department than has been the case in the past. I do not wish to hold up the committee with any further remarks, but I am satisfied that there is a case here which the government cannot refuse to recognize without placing the municipalities in the position that they will have to give inferior treatment to the Indians, or refuse them treatment altogether, or will have to assume a burden that properly belongs to the Indian Affairs branch.

I listened for a few moments this afternoon to the remarks of the hon. member for Brant. In private conversation with the hon. member he told about the Indian reservation that is in his constituency, and I believe that perhaps the Indians living there enjoy some degree of security. Unfortunately the Indians with whom I have come in contact are not in that happy position. I can only say that I consider the condition of the Indians of northern Saskatchewan to be one of the most appalling things of which I have knowledge. Up in those northern areas these people are living under the most degrading conditions. They have been degraded by the vices of the white men without having the white men's advantages. They have been treated as children and in many cases have become as children because of the treatment that has been meted out to them. Of course these people do not vote. Many hon. members do not have Indians in their ridings, but even if they have it is not considered a matter of great importance to them, simply because the Indians have no voting power. Believe me, however, from any humanitarian point of view I believe the time has come when something more should be said about our Indian people. After all, to-day there are numbers of Indian boys fighting in the armed forces of this country. I saw in the newspaper only the other day that a full-blooded Iroquois Indian had been made a general, I think, in the army of this nation. That, I am sure, will give great satisfaction to Indian people all across the country. And it points out the significant fact that where Indian people are given the advantages received by white people, or those of other races, they are capable of developing in the same way.
I know that to-day many people are very much concerned not only with the immediate winning of the war but with the implementing of the Atlantic charter in years to come. We hear references to what is going to happen to Europe, and what sort of freedom they are to have there. Perhaps Canadians, even before they begin thinking about Europe or any other part of the world, should begin to realize that it is necessary for them to do a little housecleaning so far as the Indian question in Canada is concerned. We are hoping at some time in the future to have the implementation of the Marsh report-at least, we are hoping to have some kind of new order in Canada, under which there shall be at least a basis for security for the people of our country. I submit that there is no time like the present for

Supply-Indian Affairs

taking into consideration the need for thoroughly reviewing the whole status and position of the Indians. It is many years now since the original treaties were made with the Indians in Canada. In those years we have changed considerably in our ways of thinking. Our whole manner of life has altered,, and I cannot but help think the time is ripe, as I said before, for a thorough revision. Perhaps a conference between government officials and the chiefs of Indian groups in Canada should form the basis for a revision of the existing treaties. We shall neglect our duty as Canadians if in these coming years we fail to give the Indian people in Canada the full advantage of Canadian citizenship, particularly with regard to education and health.
I fail to see why Indian children should not be given exactly the same educational facilities as any other children, and that such facilities should be provided by the government. I fail to see why, in the event of a health scheme being instituted for Canada, it should not be wide enough, sufficiently all-embracing, to include everybody. There should be no bar whatever so far as Indians are concerned.
In one corner of my constituency a new scheme has been recently established. This is not for the setting up of an Indian reserve- we already have one or two of them-but rather a reservation for the Metis people. I am wholeheartedly against the idea. I fail to see why these people should not be treated the same way as any other Canadians. Why should they be segregated? Why place them in the same position as Indians, and thereby degrade them to the same degree? We say the official policy of the government is to increase the self-respect of these people and their ability to provide for themselves. I fail to see how the segregation of the Indians or the Metis people will increase their ability to do this. They should be treated as ordinary Canadian citizens, and be given full responsibility and full advantages. If this were done, we should see a great many of them respond in an admirable manner. I would go so far as to say that as many of those Indian children would respond to decent treatment as would any other group of people in Canada. I see no difference in them whatever, except that for many years they have been relegated to an inferior position, and it has worked a most disastrous wrong upon them.
I have had correspondence recently with the minister regarding some Indians who live on the Kootenay agency in British Columbia. I have no idea why they should have written to me, but I have received communications from them to the effect that they are very unhappy about the way in which the timber

on their reservations is being handled. In his reply the minister states that this particular band of Indians have refused to give their approval to the sale of their timber for over twenty years. But they do not say that. They have gone so far as to send a petition to the Prime Minister, a copy of which I have here. It says:
We the undersigned people of the Kootenay Agency petition you as our sovereign representative and representative of the laws pertaining to our well being granted our people by the late Queen Victoria.
We have demanded an investigation into the underhand methods used by our agent in the disposal of our timber and by unbiased dominion authorities. An investigation has not been forthcoming. We make this appeal directly to you upon the basis of the evidence at a recent inquiry held at St. Mary's Indian reserve on June 2 and 3 by an inspector sent here from V ancouver.
We proclaim our loyalty and our devotion to the furthering of the war effort of our country, and in so doing appeal for public denunciation of the war effort being used as an excuse to rob our people.
We demand through you the removal of our agent who has no sympathy with nor interest in the life of our people.
This is signed by Chief Eustace, Chief Michael, Chief Luke Sam, and several other Indians, some of whom, not being able to sign their names, have made their mark. They also sent a letter to the Department of Indian Affairs, as follows:
_ We, the undersigned Indian people, under the jurisdiction of the Kootenay Indian Agency, petition our Indian Department demanding immediate cessation of timber cutting now in progress on St. Mary's Reserve, pending an immediate investigation of the method used by our agent in disposing of the timber on the St. Mary Reserve.
We declare that the methods used in disposing of the timber were underhanded and our people were subjected to duress in its disposal.
A copy of this petition is being sent to the other groups.
The same signatures appear on this letter. On this particular reservation there are vast quantities of timber, which the minister states are over-ready for cutting. I see no reason why the Indians would object to cutting the timber. They are aware of the fact that timber is needed in' the war effort. They say they are willing that it should be cut, but they have no use for the agent who, as they say, has no sympathy with or interest in the life of their people. Many agents may carry out the letter of the law and the regulations of the department, but they fail completely to have sympathy with and interest in the life of the Indian people. Such a man is not the right type of man to be in charge of an Indian agency.

I have a store bill received from an Indian *woman, with two children, and on this bill I find that she has purchased a little tea, a few dried apples, some rolled oats, 22 cents worth of cheese and a little bit of puffed wheat at a total cost of $5. Yes, $5 for herself and her two children, to live for a month. I lived once on $12 a month, and, believe me, I have not forgotten what that is like. I fail to see how we as a nation can be self-respecting people so long as we condemn any who live within the boundaries of the country to a life as degrading as this.
In his reply to me regarding these Indians in the Kootenay reservation, the minister said:
We have a right to doubt the statement that the surrender was obtained under duress. As a matter of fact we did not and do not require a surrender or the consent of the Indians to the sale.
He points out that there is an order in council governing this. I still maintain that even if there is an order in council, it is the wrong way to go about the matter. If these people were placed under an Indian agent who was sympathetic with the Indians, and who was willing to be a little more aware of their interests, he could handle the timber situation in such a way that the Indians would be satisfied to sell their timber in the manner required. I am going to ask the minister to make a further inquiry into this particular case, and send the details to me, because I do not think that three chiefs of an Indian tribe, and a great number of their followers, would sign their names to a petition like this if they had a feeling of security and faith in their Indian agent. Whatever the cause is, I do not know, but on behalf of these people I ask the minister to make an investigation and to give me further information in the matter.

The hon. member for North Battleford has not made a very practical approach to the problem she has been discussing. The difficulties encountered when dealing with Indians are largely psychological due to the fact that in a few generations the centuries-old mode of life of the Indian has been completely transformed. In the case of the reserve at Cranbrook to which my hon. friend alluded, I regret that she did not read all of my letter when she read the petition from the Indians.
I am willing to do so. It was a lengthy letter and I did not want to take the time.

The letter fully sets out the particulars. The cause of the difficulty
at Cranbrook was interference by one or two busybodies who stirred up the Indians to action that was against their own interests. This reserve has a considerable amount of timber. This was examined by competent forestry officials who advised that a certain amount of the timber should be cut in order to realize the most out of it. Anyone who is familiar with timber operations knows that you ean leave timber too long; you can leave it so long that it loses all its qualities as lumber. Undoubtedly and unquestionably that is what was taking place on this reserve. We endeavoured to get the Indians to agree to a disposal of part of this timber to an operating company on what the officers of the department considered was a fair basis. Very strict provisions were included in the agreement with the operating company to cover the manner in which the timber should be cut. One provision that I recall was that they could not cut any tree that was less than ten inches in diameter, breast high on the average man. The whole purpose of this was to apply modern and scientific principles to the cutting of timber on this particular reserve. I think I am correct in saying that if these principles are applied there will be for all the years that lie ahead a continuous source of revenue for the Indians from the timber.
Tenders were advertised for, and as I recall the successful tenderer was willing to pay a royalty, or dues, of $3.50 per thousand feet board measure. This would create a fund for the Indians in the reserve. It is true that the Indians did not want to have this action taken, as they had a feeling that their timber was being taken from them. I repeat; they were stirred up to adopt this attitude. It is not difficult on occasion to stir up Indians on matters of this kind. They felt their timber was being taken from them.

The minister has said that someone was stirring up these people. Personally I have no knowledege of the case, but I have the idea that whoever it was, he was trying to help the Indians because he felt that the Indian agent was not dealing in a proper manner. It was not stirring up the Indians at all.

I am coming to that point in a moment. At any rate the Indians resisted, and as a result the timber was deteriorating and losing its value for the Indians on the reserve. It was not desirable in the interests of the Indians, and particularly with the present need there is for lumber, that this condition of affairs should be allowed to continue. It is true the Indians have sent in a petition to the Prime Minister, with a copy

to myself and evidently a copy to the hon. member for North Battleford. It is not very difficult to get Indians to sign a petition on almost anything you want to bring up. As a matter of fact they like signing petitions It is a notorious fact that Indians, generally speaking, have a sort of love for litigation. They think there is something meritorious in being involved in matters of this kind. AH this has to be taken into account. My hon. friend has accepted the word of the Indians or of her correspondent as to the action of the agent on this reserve.
Excuse me; I merely asked for an investigation.
If my hon. friend did not accept it, then she should have looked into it more closely before bringing it up on the floor of the house.
How could anyone accept anything until a proper investigation was made? When I have a petition sent to me the least I can do is to ask for an investigation.

I think my hon. friend should have examined into the merit behind the petition before she brought it up on the floor of the house and criticized the officers of the department. This matter was fully reviewed and it was on the recommendation of the Indian commissioner for British Columbia that this action was finally taken. I think I should say that in the whole Indian administration there is not a more devoted and more intelligent official than the commissioner for Indian Affairs in British Columbia. I do not say that there may not be times when he will make a mistake, but I know that his whole purpose and effort is to serve the best interests of the Indians.
My hon. friend suggests that the matter should be further reviewed. I do not see that anything would be gained by a further review of the case. I am convinced that we have now before us and have had for some time all the essential facts in this case. I have no doubt that in a few months this agitation among the Indians will pass away. They will receive their royalty on the timber. There is also a strict provision that the operating company shall give first employment to the Indians if they are willing to take it. That would be another source of revenue to *them, and many of the Indians are particularly good at lumbering operations and the like. As I say, they will have available to them the increment that comes from the disposal of the property in the way I have mentioned.

What has
been realized from the sale of this timber?
Cutting has just started, or it may not have started yet.
Did the minister mention the name of the reserve of which he has been speaking?
It is in the Kootenay agency, near Cranbrook.
In British Columbia?
Yes.

I want to support the admirable presentation made by the member for Vancouver East in connection with the hospitals in British Columbia. I am familiar with the brief from which he largely quoted, and so far as I know it is substantially correct. The minister said of a previous speaker that she should have investigated the matter before bringing it into the house, but I think the member for Vancouver East and I myself have investigated this matter thoroughly, and the member for Vancouver East was thoroughly justified in making the suggestions which he does, in which I concur. Very often when the interests of the dominion, and the provinces or the municipalities are concerned together, we expect the dominion to get the worst end of the deal. I do not know how it is, but we would rather stick the dominion government than the province or the municipality. In this case it is the other way about. We are being cheated, to use plain bald language, by the dominion government, which refuses to pay its legal obligations and defies us. That means that we, the citizens of British Columbia, have to pay them. The dominion, and that means the citizens of Canada, have the obligation to take care of the Indians. We do not try to avoid that obligation, and we as citizens of British Columbia are prepared to pay our share through general taxaton. That is the right way to do it, taxed by the government within whose jurisdiction the Indians come, but the wrong way to do it, is to cheat the hospitals and make them get into a state of destitution so that they have to come to the general public for subscriptions -we have had to put up money before. The only alternative is to raise the rates unduly on the white people.
What I direct attention to is the utterly illogical statement, made by one government official, that the reason the dominion government could not pay a rate for the Indians comparable with the rate the white people pay was that there were no more funds and there would have to be less sickness. Those were the words the hon. member for Vancouver East quoted. I do not know how you can bring that about simply because there is
