no money. We have heard it said that people cannot afford to be sick, and I have heard it said that people cannot afford to die on account of the expense, but it is something new to hear that the Dominion of Canada cannot pay anything but a cut-throat price for the care of its wards in hospital because it has no more money. If that is the case, here and now is the place to remedy that condition. Let the minister say: "In consequence of facts that have come to my attention it will be necessary for me to ask parliament for more money for this purpose," and he would get it. But the statement was actually made by a government official: "There will have to be less sickness." Can you tell me how the Indians are to be less sick ? I myself know the case of one hospital in a town near where I live. They told us: If we did not give this unfair rate we would not get the business. My advice to that hospital board was to refuse to take the Indians in. White people are already lying in the corridors on account of the crowded state of the hospital. What is the alternative? "We will build a hospital of our own," they said. I laughed at that-building a hospital for two or three hundred cases a year. The other alternative was to take the patients out to Nanaimo, fifty-four miles away, over a mountain. The average sick person would have to be taken there in an ambulance, and any one who knows what ambulances cost will appreciate how utterly impracticable that would be when the patient might be only ten days in hospital. They were just trying to run a bluff on us.
The minister said to the last speaker that it was easy for agitators to influence the Indians. That is true. But these are white people who are not concerned at all with agitating. One man referred to, Neill-he is no relation of mine-is described as an agitator. Is anyone who asks that reasonable rates be paid an agitator? What is it the scripture says-"a little more rest, a little more sleep." The average official never wants to interfere with things as they are. Laissez-faire is his sole ambition. When somebody comes along and wants things improved, he is an agitator. All the hospital boards in British Columbia united in supporting this brief, and they asked: Why is the dominion government not paying the same price for Indians as we are paying for our white patients? And now we are told: "You have been stirred up by an agitator." All we are asking is that the dominion government should pay the same rate for Indians as we are paying for our white people. I saw the other day in the paper that the rates in the hospital to which I subscribe, to which I would go if I were sick, have been raised to make
up a deficiency in cost. Yet here is the dominion government insisting on Indians going into hospital at a price below the cost. Then they instance some remarkable hospital in the remote north which, with the aid of unpaid nuns possibly, was able to keep its rates down. But we are dealing with conditions as they are in a town where ordinary labour earns about seven or eight dollars a day, and a young boy or girl of sixteen, sixty cents an hour in a plywood mill and where nurses are working on a three-shift day.
It has been said that they are going to put up a new hospital for tubercular Indian patients near Chilliwack, that they can do it more cheaply there. It is sometimes said that the Post Office Department is run at a good profit. Cabinet ministers boast of that, but they do not tell you that half of the expense is paid out of another item and that some of the revenue comes from the stamps on our cheques, which is not revenue but a tax. Public buildings are all paid out of a separate account, yet they say: Look and behold what the post office is paying. If you investigate it, Mr. Chairman, you will find something along the same lines in regard to the hospitals. In estimating costs, they omit capital expenditure. We are not asking for something outrageous; we are not asking for anything more than is coming to us. We do not ask to be put in a preferred position. The men who drew up that brief for the united hospitals of British Columbia say: We want them to pay the same as the workmen's compensation board pays. That board does not pay more than it can help. It was stated to us when we were making representations about the matter that some of the hospitals were satisfied with this arrangement. I am willing to guarantee that none of them are satisfied. They may be quiescent, taking the attitude: "What is the use of our kicking? We are only a small hospital."
The statement has been made that the trouble has been caused by agitators and the dominion government says: We cannot afford to pay any more because we have not the funds. If that is so, the minister is now aware of it, and if he has not sufficient to pay a reasonable rate he should ask parliament for a further vote. I cannot see why individual people 'in one little community should have to pay for the losses that are caused by the hospital having to take in Indians who may come from twenty miles away. I can see no rhyme or reason in it, and if the minister says that it is because the dominion government has no funds for the purpose, I ask him to bring in a supplementary estimate if necessary for a sufficient sum. That is all we ask for

that the dominion government pay the cost of maintenance for the Indians in the hospitals to which they are sent.

A committee of which
I am a member has been investigating national health insurance and the possibility of putting on a scheme covering the whole dominion. Is it the intention of the government, if such a scheme is adopted, to include Indians? If so, the estimated cost should be noticed; it is just about twice what it is here.

Replying first to the
observation of the hon. member who has just spoken, no consideration up to the present has been given to the matter of including Indians in any health insurance scheme which may later be worked out.
Why not?

Well, I am not opposing
the idea. I am simply stating that up to the present, consideration has not been given to it. It may well be that if we embark on a national health insurance scheme the Indians will be included.
On this question of hospital rates in British Columbia, let me make it clear at once, if the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has the impression that I am guilty, that at no time have I referred to those who brought the matter to the attention of the federal government as "agitators"; I have not so described them.
I did not say so.
Then I misunderstood my hon. friend.

I said it was represented to
the minister that the matter had been gone into and that the whole thing was due to an agitator in British Columbia.

I did not quite understand my hon. friend. It may be that the department has been too parsimonious with the hospitals in British Columbia. No fault can be found with the hospitals associaton or with individual hospitals for having put before the department and before myself the representations they have made. The demands in respect of medical costs for Indians have been rising steadily. There may be those who say: Well, no matter what the demands are, you should provide a certain standard of medical care for all the Indians across Canada. I recall that this matter was discussed with myself on more than one occasion by the late Lord Tweedsmuir. He made a trip on one occasion to Aklavik, and he thought that our hospital facilities in the far northern country were deficient, that we did not have the proper

hospital facilities there. But when we come to administer the funds voted by parliament we try to get the maximum of results. Certainly if we have x dollars for hospital treatment of Indians and the rate is, say, $2.50 a day, you can care for more Indians than if the rate is $3 a day. I am not just now justifying the department. It may be that our attitude to this matter is not wise. But certainly when you have in mind the tremendous demands for the spending of public money in all directions and the need of maintaining some sort of balance in our economy, consideration has to be given to matters such as this.
As I recall, the rates complained of in British Columbia were $2.50 a day. We have, for most of the hospitals in that province, and I think it will apply very shortly to all of them, raised the rate to $2.75 a day. The hospitals association wished the rate fixed at S3 per day, and I shall be glad, in the light of the representations made here by the hon. members who have spoken to the matter, to take it into further consideration. I think this request has come from all hon. members from British Columbia irrespective of their political affiliations. I might point out, however, that in the operation of our own hospitals, in which we have some experience, we managed to carry them on at a figure substantially below the rate we pay the general public hospitals. For example, we have in British Columbia a hospital at Coqualeetza which was brought into operation about August 1, 1941. It is mainly concerned with tuberculosis. From August 1, 1941, to December 31, 1942, a period of seventeen months, there were 457 patients at one time or another, there were 52,253 hospital days, and the per diem cost was $2.08 per day.

Did that include capital
expenditure?
No, I was just going to refer to that. I intended to make it clear that that does not include items of taxes or depreciation or interest on the money invested.
Capital expenditures.
Referring to another government operated hospital, that at Qu'Appelle, in Saskatchewan, there, 1,349 pa/tients were treated, with a total of 28.114 hospital days, and a per diem cost of $1.33.
For what period?
That would cover a year, I think.

Which year?

Supply-Indian Affairs

Well, probably the last
year for which we have records. It would be the last audited statement.

What about comparable
wages? Has the minister any record?

We engage the nurses and all other help, and we have to pay them the proper rates in order to retain them. Let me make it clear that I am not putting forward these facts as an argument against the requests made this afternoon on this point. All I wish to say is that in the light of the representations a full review will be made of the matter. At any rate the rate will be $2.75 in British Columbia, and I hope we shall be able to get it raised to $3.

With reference to the Indian situation in Nova Scotia, I am familiar with it up to about three months ago. I carried on considerable correspondence with the department and met departmental officials. The programme in that province is to concentrate the Indians at two particular points, Eskasoni and Shubenacadie. I am not going to say anything about the merits or the demerits of the scheme. What I am interested in is this. You are making good progress in concentrating them at these two points and you run into the priorities board with respect to the necessary materials to build houses in the areas in which you are going to complete your programme. That was the situation up to three months ago. I do not know anything about it beyond that point. All I want the minister to do is to give me a brief summary of matters as they now stand. Has he developed his programme? Is he getting materials for the necessary buildings in order to complete the programme he has in Nova Scotia?

That comes under another vote, but I can answer it now. Steps were initiated about two years ago looking to the concentration of Indians in Nova Scotia on two reserves. There were roughly 2,000 Indians scattered over nineteen reserves without proper supervision. Some of the reserves were close to towns and cities and that made it difficult to achieve any real progress with the Indians. They are being gathered together in these two reserves, and that involves the building of houses, schools and teachers' residences, because our aim is to secure teachers who will remain permanently on the reserve and thus acquire influence with the Indians. Tenders have been called for these buildings, and it is not expected that we shall have any difficulty in getting the materials necessary for their construction.

I suggest that if the minister proposes a change of rates in hospital pay they be uniform throughout the whole dominion. Costs for hospitalization are comparable in all provinces, and it would be poor policy to single out British Columbia or any other province and fix one rate there and another rate in some other province.

We seem to be having a general discussion on this item, and I should like to direct a few questions to the minister with reference to a matter of some importance. The first question is what attitude the government has taken with reference to the calling of Indians for military service. The minister knows that there has been some discussion as to the exact status of the Indians in the matter of military service. Sessional paper No. 136J, brought down in the house on Thursday, June 24, contains two letters to Indian agents in Saskatchewan. I should like to quote briefly from these. The first letter is from the general superintendent of Indian agencies to Mr. J. R. Favel, Sweet Grass Indian Reserve, Prongua, Saskatchewan. I quote:
Dear Sir:
I have your letter of December 8 with respect to compulsory service of Indians.
In your letter you have pointed out that you are quite positive that Indians, or anyone who is not enfranchised, are not subject to service.
We are not interpreters of the law here and the only reply I can make to this is that in a letter we received from our branch at Ottawa the following was drawn to my attention:-
"The national -war services department has now advised that all Indians must hold themselves in readiness for call for military service (30 daj-s' training). If the Indians desire to avoid this military service, representations must be made by them, individually, when they are called for their medical examination. The representations would 'then be forwarded to Ottawa and would be considered at that time."
Yours truly,
M. Christianson, General Superintendent of Indian Agencies.
The second letter is also from the general superintendent of Indian agencies to Chief and Councillors, Little Pine Reserve, Paynton, Saskatchewan. The letter is file No. 302-5. I will not quote more than two paragraphs:
In this connection I wish to inform you that shortly after I came back to Regina in 1940, I brought this very same matter to the attention of His Honour, Mr. Justice Embury, chairman of the national war services board, and he looked thoroughly into the matter of the enlistment of Indians in the Canadian army. His Honour Mr. Justice Embury informed me that he could find nothing in the treaties of Canada with the Indians whereby they were exempt from military service. At the same time he explained to me that the Indians could
Supply-Indian Affairs

not be called for military service overseas, but they could be drafted for the army for service in Canada only.
During the last war a number of Indians all over the country were conscripted. At that time the government found that an error had been made and treaty Indians could not be conscripted for overseas service in the army as that promise had been made to them at the time of the signing of the treaties, that is, they could not be conscripted for fighting wars outside of Canada, therefore those Indians who had been conscripted were discharged immediately from the army.
I should like to know first whether that is a correct interpretation, that the Indians can be conscripted for service in Canada, and second, whether they can be conscripted for service abroad. What is the exact legal status of the Indian who is called for service in Canada? As wards of the government, without the full rights of citizenship, does the government contemplate giving them some of the rights of citizenship in view of the fact that they are discharging some of its responsibilities? I should like to have that clarified because a number of Indians have been confused on this question.
I have another question to ask the minister with reference to a matter that was brought up in the house on May 24, as reported on page 2930 of Hansard. I had a question on the order paper as follows:
Has a letter been issued by the superintendent of Indian agencies at Regina, notifying the Indians that only part of the interest accruing from money held in trust will be paid to the Indians during the war?
The answer to that question was:
No. An attempt has, however, been made through inspectors and Indian agents to persuade Indians to forgo temporarily, in whole or in part, the distribution of interest earnings and other moneys held in trust for them.
The minister goes on to explain that the Indians have better opportunities for earning money now, and states that it is not felt that they are in great need of money, some of which is being withheld from them. I have had complaints from Indians in the reserves immediately around Regina that moneys accruing to them from trust funds have been withheld without their consent or consultation with them. That statement may not be correct, but I should like the minister to state to the committee whether or not, in the event of the Indians not agreeing to having this money which is coming to them withheld temporarily, either in whole or in part, it is the policy of the Indian administration to withhold that money on a compulsory basis. When I was in the west some of the Indians told me that they had received this year only about forty per cent of the money which they were accustomed [Mr. T. C. Douglas.!
to receiving in other years and that they had never at any time been asked whether or not they would agree to have any money withheld,
I agree with the minister that there are cases where some Indians have more money than they had before. Some of them have sons in the army or some of the women have husbands and are therefore getting dependent's allowance. But there are other cases where the war has not made much difference. I met one man who has a large family and who is operating a small farm, and his expenses are as great as they ever were. His cost of living is higher and the fact that money is withheld constitutes a severe financial problem for him.
These are the questions I should like to have the minister answer, first of all with reference to the status of the Indians in the matter of compulsory military service, and second, whether or not this money is withheld from them without their consent.

In regard to the first question, the hon. member was not in earlier when I answered a similar question from the other side of the house, but I may briefly repeat the answer. Indians are liable to military service in the same -way as any other citizen of the country. The justice department gave a ruling to that effect. They are British subjects and consequently are treated alike in the matter of military service with all other British subjects The view of the Department of Justice was supported by a court decision not very long ago in the Montreal district.
With regard to the second question, it is not necessary to secure the consent of the Indians to the withholding of funds, as for instance the interest on band funds, unless there is some understanding to the contrary. I have in mind the case where some of the assets of a band may be sold. If the Indians gave their consent to the disposal of the assets on certain terms, those terms would have to be observed, but in the cases my hon. friend has in mind consent is not necessary. The officers of the department, who are wholly sympathetic to Indian welfare generally, in the cases cited felt that the Indians were not in need of the funds at that particular time. If $500 is coming to an Indian as the result of a fur catch, for example, and he gets that $500, I venture to say that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the money will disappear within thirty days. It is much better to hold the funds and distribute them to the Indian as his need arises. As a matter of fact that is what is being done in connection with some of the fur reserves that were set up

Supply-Indian Affairs
and are now in operation, with the result that in some cases we have been able to pay an Indian family $20 or $25 a month the year round. It is much better to hold back the money and pay it in monthly instalments of that kind than to give the family a lump sum of $240 or $300.
I can assure my hon. friend that it is the desire of those administering Indian affairs to deal equitably and justly, though perhaps at times it must be done firmly, with the Indians under their administration.

I want to make just one comment in reference to the minister's reply. Has the government given any thought to the proposition that if these Indians are to be held to be British subjects and therefore subject to the responsibilities of citizenship, they should enjoy some of the rights of citizenship? It seems to me that if in the matter of military service the government now is going to say that the Indians are British subjects, we should give some consideration to extending the franchise to them and giving them some of the privileges of British subjects. That might not be done all at once, but certainly I think we should not ask them to pay the price and accept the responsibility without giving them some of the privileges.
I fully agree with the minister when he says that where a large sum of money is coming to the Indians it is much better to spread the payment of that money over a period of time; I think that is a very wise procedure. The Indians I have in mind, however, and the ones to whom I spoke, had no such sums coming to them. I remember one man who usually had about $100 or $110 coming to him as the interest on some funds held in trust. This year he was given only about $40. He was counting on that money' to buy seed to get ready for spring operations, and $40 was totally inadequate to meet his needs. It seems to me that these matters should be handled on an individual basis rather than under any blanket regulation. There might be certain cases in which the withholding of the money would be the best possible thing for the families concerned, while in other cases it might be a hardship. If the practice of withholding money has been adopted as a general policy I suggest that the department may be working an undue hardship on some of these Indians. It seems to me the cases ought to be investigated and dealt with individually, on the basis of the individual need.

If my hon. friend will give me the individual case he has in mind I shall be very glad to have full particulars
supplied to him. As a matter of fact generally speaking the cases are dealt with individually ratiher than en bloc. With regard to enfranchisement, to which my hon. friend refers, a comparatively small number of Indians are enfranchised each year. There is a peculiar thing about this, however; if the hon. member for Brant were here no doubt he could give us some information on it. On many of these reserves where the Indians could be enfranchised they do not want it, and of course there is no compulsion exercised by the authorities. It may be that in the years that lie ahead the question of compulsory enfranchisement, that is, compulsorily making the Indians citizens of the country in the ordinary sense, may have to be considered. My experience and observation, however, give me the impression that many of the Indians who would be quite competent to exercise the franchise would refuse to accept it. This situation may arise from a mistaken idea of their peculiar status. Some of these Indian bands say, "We are allies of Canada; we are an allied nation within the Canadian nation." All I can say is that it has not been the practice compulsorily to enfranchise any Indians, and that as a matter of fact a great many who would be quite capable of exercising the franchise would refuse to accept it.
It might be wise to give them ah opportunity to avail themselves of it.
They have that opportunity now.

Item agreed to.
Immigration branch-
169. Field and inspectional service abroad, $80,004.

May I take a moment of the committee's time to mention that Mr. F. C. Blair who has been associated with the immigration branch for almost forty years has reached retirement age; indeed retirement age was reached a few years ago, but I was able to prevail upon him to remain. I just wish to say that in all my experience with government officials I have known none more conscientious or more faithful in the discharge of his duties. He brought to the discharge of these duties ability of a very high order. I simply wish to pay this tribute to a public official who has rendered long and distinguished service to his country.

Mr. Chairman, the words so well expressed by the minister find a ready echo on this side of the house. It would have been unfortunate had the services
Supply-Immigration

and record of Mr. Blair gone unnoticed, or without tribute at this time. I join with the minister, and express on behalf of this party an appreciation of the services Mr. Blair has so loyally, so industriously and with such capacity rendered to Canada.
On the matter of immigration, 'has the government given, or is it giving consideration to a policy of immigration for Canada at the close of the war? This is a question which for a considerable time has engaged the attention of people across Canada. We are now in a time of war. We have found that unpreparedness for war has been a costly business, and I think it is only fair to point out that it will be equally costly not only in dollars and cents but in many other respects if, at the dawning of an era of peace, we find ourselves unprepared, as we were unprepared for war. Is the minister in a position to-day to give the committee any indication of what policy the government intends to follow with respect to post-war immigration to Canada?

Consideration is being
given to this problem continuously, as well as to other post-war problems. However, I am sure my hon. friend will recognize that at the present time it is difficult to lay down any definite plans which, it could be said, would be closely followed. We have yet to conclude the war. We have yet to see what sort of peace will be worked out when the war is over. In the light of the conditions then prevailing, and the information that will then be available, more definite decisions can be taken as to what public policy in this regard should be.

I hope the question of
immigration will not be left entirely until the peace treaty has been signed between the warring nations of the world.

As I have told my hon.
friend, the matter is constantly under consideration.

Item agreed to.
Soldier settlement of Canada-
336. Administration of soldier settlement and British family settlement, $542,930.

I believe it is less than twenty-five years since the conclusion of the last war. We have already fought almost four years in this war. From present indications great war No. 1 was only a patch on the one we are now fighting. While we have been trying to rectify

things throughout the world, I feel we have failed to improve the conditions of some of the victims, if I may so describe them, of the first great war. I refer to the soldier settlers.
I am sorry we have not been given an opportunity earlier in the session to discuss this matter. Again this year we are following the procedure adopted last year, namely, that of crowding estimates to the value of millions of dollars into the dying hours of the session. I should like to read an address delivered by Sir Robert Borden to the Canadian expeditionary force in 1917, and having done so, I shall inquire whether Canada has fulfilled the promises therein set out, the promises by the then Prime Minister to the men who fought the war of 1914-18. He said:
You are men actually facing the enemy day and night. You are suffering greatly from fatigue, over-strain, and lack of rest. The marvel of it is that men could undergo such a strain without breaking; but you have never yet broken, and history will appreciate that in days to come.
You men are about to enter one of the most serious engagements that ever faced the Canadian corps. I cannot, at this moment, give any information as to where this attack will be staged, whether it be successful or not, it is to be borne in mind that it will not be an easy success. ... We feel confident that you will succeed where others failed; for you have never yet failed in anything you have set your hand to, as a Canadian corps.
You can go into this action feeling assured of this, and as the head of the government, I give you this assurance; that you need have no fear that the government and the country will fail to show just appreciation of your service to the country and empire in what you are about to do and what you have already done.
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home, and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion, that the country will support the government to prove to the returned man its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire; and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken with the men who won and the men who died.

I take it my hon. friend
desires to make a somewhat extended speech. In that event I would ask that the item stand so that we may proceed with the Department of Public Works. I understand that the minister of that department has an engagement which he must keep.
Item stands.

256. Departmental administration, $194,780.

I do not know whether the matter I have in mind comes under this item; but, if not, I hope the minister will see that my remarks are called to the attention of the appropriate minister. In these days of common-sense dress, especially during the summer time, I do not think our protective staff and others in the building should have to dress as they do during the warm weather. The heavy clothing they must wear is not only uncomfortable but, to my mind, it is not healthy. I believe something has been promised by way of relief for the protective staff, but something should also be done for the elevator operators.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The protective staff comes
under the jurisdiction of the Speaker, and I shall be glad to inform him of what the hon. member for New Westminster has said. We are considering making a change in the uniforms worn by the elevator operators in the building.

Last year on the orders of the day I asked the Minister of Public Works if anything was contemplated in the way of flood control works on the Higbwood river which passes through the town of High River, some distance south of Calgary. At that time we were in what is lightly known as the flood season. Snow collects to great depths in the foothills and in the Rocky mountains throughout the southern part of Alberta, and at certain seasons of the year, especially when the warm rains come, the water rushes down the streams and rivers at such a terrific rate that very often towns are in serious danger of being flooded out. That is exactly what happened on that occasion.
Some debris and stones and wood had gathered in 'the bed Of the river sufficiently to change the channel of the river, resulting in the town of High River being under water. Damage to the extent of many thousands of dollars was done. These floods are of such a nature that this town is not only in dangeT of suffering great property damage, but they come with such suddenness that there is also a danger of loss of life. Since that time this community has had to face a further danger. Flood conditions were not so bad this year because some little work had been done, and perhaps the rains came at different times or were not so severe and the ice jams were not as great. The attention of the department was drawn to this matter and I asked the department to place an appropriation in the estimates this year to cover this work.
When I got the estimates this year I found appropriations of millions of dollars but nothing for this work. I have interviewed the minister and the town of High River has sent representatives to Ottawa to interview the government. I should like to give credit to the Hon. Senator Riley for what he has done to urge the government to make an appropriation for this particular work. I scan through the estimates and I find the following appropriations for the different provinces:
Nova Scotia	 $450,900
Prince Edward Island	 45,000
New Brunswick	 80,000
Quebec	 387,500
Ontario	 151,000
Manitoba	      20,000
Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories	 10,000
British Columbia and Yukon		345,300
Nearly $13,000,000 are being appropriated for public works, but not one penny is being provided for this work in the town of High River. I have never asked this department or the government for very much. I will tell the minister now that when I do ask for anything it will be because what I am asking for is positively andi absolutely necessary. I happen to represent a constituency in which there is very little need of federal appropriation, except for wheat acreage reduction bonus or something of that kind. I have very little need to ask the government for appropriations for public works. I do not have any federal government institutions in my constituency except two small customs offices and the regular post offices. Therefore I do not think I am asking too much when I come to the department and state the case of this community which is in grave danger of suffering considerable property damage, if not of being swept out of existence. I do not think I am asking very much when I come to the department for just a few thousand dollars to do this work that must be done on the Highwood river for the prevention of floods.
I hold in my hand an aerial photograph taken by the Royal Canadian Air Force official photographer as his plane flew over the site. I pass this photograph over to the minister so that he may see for himself what the town looks like. The photograph shows only part of the town, but if the minister will look at it very carefully, he will notice under one of the bridges a rushing torrent, with the water mounting almost up to the floor of the bridge. The bridges are still in, despite the fact that the river has overflowed its banks. He will notice, too, that part of the railroad is completely under water, that the highway is completely under water, and that the streets are
Supply-Public Works

completely under water. I am sure he could not tell me where the banks of the river are, because it looks as though there were half a dozen rivers in there, but actually there is only one river, the whole town being under water.
There are one or two important features connected with this flood. It is through this town that the main trunk highway leads from the United States north to the Alaska highway. The one hard-surfaced paved highway that links the United States with the Alaska highway to the north runs through this very town of High River, which, as this picture shows, is completely under water.
Another important consideration that I would bring to the minister's attention is that there is a Royal Canadian Air Force training school adjacent to this community. It is not shown in the picture; it is about a mile to the left hand side of the picture. I do not know what the contour of the land is at the air school, but I have been told1 that the school is in danger at the high-water season.
I know the argument may be: This is not altogether our responsibility; the provincial authorities have some responsibility in the matter. I am not going to deny that, but what I do say is that at a time when floods are so serious it is no use and there is no time to wrangle over responsibility. One thing I am certain of is that this government cannot escape responsibility for floods wherever they may occur in Canada, because floods mean danger to the life of the citizens of Canada.
The provincial government of Alberta have done considerable work this year on this project. I was going to quote from the High River Times a resolution which the town of High River sent on to the provincial government of Alberta commending them for the work they had done, but evidently I did not bring it down with me. The town council of High River passed a resolution and forwarded it to the provincial government commending them for what they had done this year on the project. But this government has done nothing. I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were willing to make some donation to this work, realizing that their line was in some danger on account of these flood conditions. If a private concern such as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is willing to contribute; if the engineering staff of the department of public works of the Alberta government is at the disposal of the town of High River, and if the town of High River is itself willing to contribute its share to this project, I think it is 
not too much for me to ask the federal government to bear some share of the financial burden of this work.
We are calling upon our people to do a good deal of sacrificing in these days, and I am wondering now if this government is willing to show the people of this district that it is willing to sacrifice on their behalf. Surely this government cannot escape some responsibility in the matter. As I say, we ask the people to sacrifice, and they do. This community has done its share of sacrificing and of making donations to cause after cause, and in taking its share of victory bonds. I do not want to be too harsh, but I wish to read a clipping from the High River Times of April 1, 1943, -written at a time when the town was in danger from flood this spring. I do not want the minister to consider this article too hot. I want him to recognize as I read it that at the time it was written the people of that community were in danger of losing life and property. The article reads:
Since the outbreak of war this town and district have supported every appeal the federal government has issued. Approximately $600,000 have gone from here for victory bonds.
I pause for a moment to say that was the figure after the third victory loan campaign and it has been very considerably increased by the contributions to the fourth victory loan. I continue the quotation:
Every other form of financial appeal has been similarly supported. This is a relatively prosperous settlement and the federal government receives substantial contribution from our citizens by way of income tax and an infinity of other taxes.
The town and district have sent out hundreds of the best young people to the call of the armed services. Now, in the time of community need Ottawa refuses every appeal to preserve what has been built up.
Yet the consequences of delayed action are likely to be infinitely more costly. If the river is permitted to fulfil its present threats, High River citizens will ibe in no position to buy victory bonds nor pay income tax nor respond to any requests and demands of the federal government. In fact there may easily be the problem of reestablishment of flood victims, a relief problem far transcending the $25,000 which is asked. In addition both governments may face losses in the whole area of the Little Bow in public roads, bridges, homes, farm lands and so on.
At that particular season, namely the spring season, people in the town of High River and district are really facing reality when the ice jam takes place in the river, and it can easily take place when rains begin to come on the mountains and there is still ice in the river. Flood conditions can be extremely serious. The rush of water is bad. It breaks down dams; it uproots trees, and life is in danger. If any lives were lost in a
JULY 23, m3
Supply-Public Works
flood, the government would immediately demand some sort of an inquiry. An inquiry would be made, decisions reached, and apologies made. But apologies would then be too late. If something -is not done conditions may be serious in the future. I must be fair and say to the minister that the Alberta government has done considerable work this year, and we trust that the danger of serious damage by reason of flood may have passed by reason of such work, but still more is necessary. I will not delay the committee farther, but I ask the minister to give me and the committee and the people of that community an answer to the effect that his department will consider placing in next year's estimates, in plenty of time, an item of twenty or twenty-five thousand dollars for this work. I know what happens with these estimates. I know that a department likes to place a number of items there; that they go before the treasury board and that the board take out their blue pencils and mark out this and mark out that and mark out something else. I do not know who the members of the treasury board will be next year, whether there will be any change, but I urge the minister to include this item in next year's estimates and impress upon the board with all the determination, persuasiveness and enthusiasm of which he is capable, that the item for this particular purpose shall be left in. Can I get an assurance from the minister that some consideration will be given along this line?

I would be the last man to blame the hon. member for Macleod for explaining the flood situation at High River. If the same condition existed in my riding, probably I would make the same speech as he has just made. I really sympathize with these people, and I have received representations on their behalf from the hon. member and the senator of that district. I am glad that we agree that these damages do not fall under the responsibility of the federal government. We have no jurisdiction over mountain streams or floods. I was most sympathetic when the hon. member spoke to me about this, but I could not find any way to have an estimate placed in the present vote.
The government controls all the money.

Were this department to provide estimates in respect of all damages caused by floods we would have to meet a considerable number of requests. I might point out that in the last two or
three weeks there was a flood in the province of Quebec which caused damages amounting to over a million dollars.

Mr. Chairman, might I interrupt? I am not asking the minister to reimburse the citizens of High River for damage done; I am asking for an appropriation to carry on the work of directing the channel of the river so that floods will not occur again. I believe that, if the minister does not quite understand the situation, his deputies and engineers are well acquainted with the facts. I repeat that the citizens of High River do not ask for any compensation from the department because their homes were damaged, the cellars flooded, the mains broken up; they are asking only for an appropriation for work to be done in the river so that the channel will be safeguarded.

Were I to try to comply with the request, I would have to comply with requests made from other parts of the country where they have floods. My engineers, who understand the situation, inform me that we have absolutely no jurisdiction.
Is this a navigable river?
No; it is a mountain stream.
It is a creek.
It is no creek.

Although I am most sympathetic, I could not commit the department or the government to promising that we shall have an estimate next year for this purpose. I believe certain grants have been made for protection works along rivers; but since the beginning of the war it has been the policy of the government, and it has been demanded by all opposition parties, that civil estimates should be reduced as much as possible. This year there is a decrease of $405,000. I do not feel at liberty to start increasing at this time our civil estimates. It would be absolutely contrary to the policy of the government, and I do not believe I would receive the support of the opposition were we to come in with large estimates for other things at the present time.
Is that a factor which is usually taken into consideration?

That is what I am trying to take into consideration in preparing my own estimates. Perhaps I am wrong. I would rather vote large sums of money to all constituencies, were I at liberty
Supply

Public Works

to do so, but I do not think I would receive the support or approval of the house if I tried to change the policy at the present time.

Chief engineer's branch-
Maintenance and operation of graving docks, locks and dams, etc.-
285. Snagboats, $49,745.

When this item was up last year I asked the then Minister of Public Works what effort was being made to have the snags taken out of the Athabaska river between Waterways and Chippewyan. That river had many snags in it, roots and butts of trees lying in the water, which caused a great deal of damage to the boats going down it; frequently the bottoms of either the barges or the towboats were damaged. Has the department any appliance on the Athabaska river for removing these snags?

We had the engineers of the department investigate the complaint in regard to snags on the Athabaska river, and after we received their report we had some dreding done which helped to relieve the situation. We have no snagboat on the Athabaska river; the only two snag-boats we have are on the Fraser and Skeena rivers in British Columbia. We have received no complaints lately about snags, though we communicated with the different companies operating on the Athabaska river. If the situation warrants any action, I am sure the department will do its utmost to remedy any difficulties.
If there is not a vote for removing the snags from the Athabaska river then the department should have one.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-
290. Generally, $20,975.
Are there any specially large items under this vote, described as "generally"?

The largest
amount would be for the Portage du Fort bridge, an interprovincial bridge between Quebec and Ontario, amounting to 83,500, and an amount of 87,000 for the Perley bridge at Hawkesbury. Those are the two largest.

Why does the minister build his items in this fashion? I notice that he has an item of only $3,050 for bridges and approaches in Ottawa, but under this general item he has these two larger expenditures. In order that the committee shall be fully
Supply-Public Works

informed of the details I do not think the minister should follow a system which, in fact, is not really a system at all.
It is a system which existed long before I came to the department.
That is scarcely a real answer.
It could not be excused, of course, if it is not a correct practice. The officials have not changed their minds up to now. However, I can give greater detail with respect to this vote.
The point which concerns me is that in this general vote there are amounts larger than the amount voted for Ottawa bridges and approaches.
I see an item here amounting to $150 for the Calumet bridge, and-

The minister has missed my point entirely. I am not desirous of having these small amounts placed on record, but I am desirous of having amounts specified when they are greater than the amounts contained in detailed items. I cannot quite see why the committee is not entitled to have these larger amounts in detail, rather than in bulk form.
Perhaps the leader of the opposition is right in what he says, but there are only two items larger than the item for Ottawa, and they are the ones I have mentioned.

I have no complaint so far as the smaller items are concerned; in fact I think it is quite proper that they be submitted in bulk; but I still fail to see the wisdom of detailing the item for Ottawa, and then placing these larger items in a bulk vote. I raise this point as a caution to the minister that when he brings his estimates down again-if he has that opportunity-he ought to see that the procedure I have suggested is adopted.
I shall call it to the attention of my .officials.

Item agreed to.
Ontario

295. Port Maitland-dredging-(revote, $12,800), $21,100.
Harbours and rivers generally-for maintenance of services, no new works to be undertaken, $130,000.

I notice in this item an amount for dredging at Port Maitland, part of which is a revote. Is this work completed? The

summer is fairly well advanced, and I know a dredge was there waiting to do the work. I ask this question because a large amount of material is being removed from the bed of the river, and along the harbour there is a breakwater behind which there is a certain amount of filling to be done. I took this matter up last fall with the department, but owing to the fact that the dredge was not properly constructed to force the dirt over the retaining wall I was told the work could not be done. Has any further consideration been given to the matter?
I am informed that the contract will be completed in about a month's time, and this amount is for the completion.

I understand that. I think there is enough material removed from the bed of the river to fill it in. At present it is being thrown into the lake. It is essential that this work should be done, namely, that of filling in behind the retaining wall, because there is nothing behind that wall to hold it. It is just standing under its own strength. On the other hand, if it had dirt behind it to keep it from any possible buckling in, it would be much better. I was told at the time that owing to the construction of the dredge which, I believe, opened at the bottom and let the material drop into the lake, it was not possible to do the work. The board of trade and chamber of commerce of the village of Dunn-ville have been anxious to have this matter looked into.
I am informed that we are saving enough filling to make the backfill behind the retaining wall. That will be done.

Item agreed to.
Telegraph branch-
S00. Telephone service at Ottawa, $100,000.

There is a very large
increase in telephone service in Ottawa, largely owing, of course, to war-time conditions. I fancy the increase in the number of lines and the service in governmental departments has increased many times over and above the normal peace-time service. Has the government made any agreement with the telephone company for any special rates, in view of the large number of services installed?

This amount is to pay the cost of the telephone services maintained in the government departments in Ottawa, but it does not cover telephones in the war departments.

Supply-Public Works
Does the government get a special rate in view of the large amount of service they take?

We have a special rate which is much lower than the ordinary business or residential rate. The residential rate is S3.37 a month; private branch exchange, $3.97; office, $4.84. In September, 1939, we had 1,900 telephones in Ottawa; to-day we have
8,000.	Three-quarters of these telephones are used by departments primarily engaged in military matters. Then it has been necessary to make thousands of transfers of telephones within the same buildings and also to new buildings where departments have been assigned space. Under the war appropriation we had an item of $300,000 for telephones. This vote takes care of 2,060 peace-time telephones, whereas the $300,000 vote takes care of the remainder.

When I first came to Ottawa the telephones in the members' offices were kept connected during the recess. It is of great convenience when a member comes to Ottawa during the summer months to be able to go to his office and make any appointments he may want to make with departmental officials. But to-day our telephones are cut off and we cannot get our work done as expeditiously. It should not cost very much to leave these telephones connected for the remainder of the year.
Mr. MoCANN: The matter which the hon. member for Haldimand referred to is the very matter I wished to speak to myself. Telephone service apparently comes under the Department of Public Works. As the hon. member has said, we are here for approximately six months in the year and those members who are close to Ottawa and have to make visits here during the recess would find it convenient if their telephones were still connected. I suggest to the minister that the matter of telephone service in the House of Commons should be in the hands of the Speaker or the Clerk of the House. I think either one of these gentlemen would exercise reasonable care and good judgment as to what telephones should be left connected.

May I join with the two hon. members who have spoken. It has proved most inconvenient for many members when they come to Ottawa during the recess to find their telephones not connected. Does this vote cover the ordinary service charges, or does it cover long distance calls as well?

This is for service only.
In connection with the other matter, if an hon. member expects to spend any time in Ottawa during the recess, all he needs to do is to apply to the Clerk of the House in order to have his telephone connected. In years gone by we spent as much as three or four thousand dollars a year in order to keep the telephones connected in all the rooms.

There is a feeling abroad that a lot of reckless long-distance telephoning is done by government departments, and I suggest that the minister check in his own department. However, I do not suggest that his department is the subject of this complaint. It is an easy thing to form the habit of calling long distance if the government is paying the bill. The long-distance telephone should not be used with reckless abandon in order to make calls from one end of the country to the other, perhaps not always on government business, although I make no such charge.

Long-distance
calls are paid for by each department and we have no control over calls other than those made by our own department. The Department of Public Works is carrying on works and repairs from Halifax to Vancouver and, when emergencies arise, the long-distance telephone is probably used. I do not know that there is any extravagance in this connection.
Would it be possible for a person in the minister's department to make a personal long-distance call?
A list of calls is made up every month and I believe the object of each call must be stated.

Item agreed to.
Chief architect's branch-
Construction, repairs and improvements-public buildings-*
Nova Scotia-
502. Shelburne-Public building additions, $7,000.
May I ask the minister what this public building is used for and why the addition is being made?

This amount is required to provide for the construction of a one-storey brick addition thirty feet long by eighteen feet wide at the rear of the building for the purpose of providing increased accommodation for the Post Office Department.

Last session I inquired of the minister and the Postmaster General whether it would be possible to get an amount in the
Supply-Public Works

estimates to provide a suitable post office building in a town of 12,000 to 13,000 people in my constituency in place of the ramshackle building that is now being used for a post office at Dominion, Nova Scotia. It is a disgrace to the name of post office. The minister stated at the time that it was not the policy, for the duration of the war at least, to do any new construction or make repairs that would involve considerable expenditure. In view of this vote I wish to ask the minister if the departments have changed their policy. If so, does it leave the door open for the redress of the grievance I raised last session in connection with the disgraceful conditions at the post office building in the town of Dominion, Nova Scotia.

It is the policy of the department not to build new post offices during the war. We never spend money for post offices without a request from the Post Office Department. They needed additional space in Shelburne, and I have here a letter which formed the basis of our decision. The chief superintendent of the post office service made this recommendation:
The postmaster at the Shelburne post office finds it increasingly difficult to maintain an efficient and satisfactory service. This is due to the ever-increasing volume of postal business undertaken at this point and the limited working space which the postmaster has at his disposal.
One of the chief reasons for the increase in the volume of business is due to the strength of army formations stationed at this centre and, in view of the presence of these military units, it is very essential that the efficientcy of the postal service be maintained.
Last year the Department of National Revenue was good enough to loan to this department a room formerly used by them as an examining warehouse. Recently, however, they were obliged to ask for the return of this room in view of increased customs activities at this point.
Taking all these factors into consideration it is apparent that there is no alternative but to request the erection of an addition to this building and in this connection I beg to attach a sketch showing the proposed addition.
As the necessity for this additional space is in a great measure due to the presence of military units, it is felt that the cost of the work of the addition could properly be charged to war appropriation.

I am not quarrelling with this vote at all. I approve it, but I am trying to point out exactly the same conditions obtain in the post office at Dominion. There is a lack of space, and inefficient service on account of that lack of space, in the building called the post office, a building that is a disgrace to the postal service. I dropped the matter last session after the minister had assured me that it was not the intention of the department for

the duration of the war to make any expenditures in that direction. This vote is a departure from that policy, and I am inquiring if the road is now open to having repairs made at other places where they are badly needed, or else does the change of policy apply only to certain parts of the country?

We never make alterations of this kind unless the Post Office Department recommends them and they are helpful to the war effort. I do not know the details of the case my hon. friend has put forward. It has not come to my knowledge.
It has come to the department's knowledge forcibly on more than one occasion, but not while the minister has held that porfolio.
I shall look into the matter to see if something should be done, but I can give no assurance to the hon. member without having all the facts before me.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch
Dredging-Nova Scotia
507. Canso-To purchase and repair wharf,

I understand that some investigation has been carried on by the engineering branch of the Department of Public Works into the possibilities of building a causeway across the strait of Canso. Is anything being done in that direction? If there is such a possibility, expenditure on wharves might be unnecessary, because a causeway across the strait of Canso would alter the whole present set-up and much of it would be eliminated. Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-Dredging-Ontario-
509. Grand river-Final agreed contribution to improvements; the Grand river conservation commission to discharge the crown from all claims whatsoever connected therewith and to undertake to pay to the dominion government, upon receipt thereof, 37 J per cent of net proceeds of any sale of lands and buildings, of any refund of money® from the Canadian Pacific Railway and of any moneys realized from capital investments, $59,325.45.

This amount refers to
the cost of the building of the Shand dam, does it not?
Right.
Three or four miles north of Fergus. How much has the government contributed1 as its share of the cost of the Shand dam?

Is the query
concerning the amount paid by the government toward this project?
Yes.
It is $769,318.68, or up till March 31, 1941, the figure was $709,993. This is the final payment.
What is the total amount the government has already paid out?
It is $709,993.23. This amount of $59,325.45 is the final payment on the agreement.

This afternoon the hon.
member for Macleod made some reference to flood-proofing the High river in Alberta. The Department of Public Works will now have, in the flood-proofing of the Grand river, an example of the benefits of flood-proofing rivers. There would have been a large flood this year on the Grand river but for the Shand dam.
Unfortunately there was.

The Shand dam prevented this spring a flood in the Grand valley which, the press of the valley stated, would have cost a very large sum of money. So that the money expended on this operation, which completes the government part of the Shand
dam, is money well spent. The Ontario government have put up just as much. They were to pay 37^ per cent too. The municipalities of Brantford, Galt and the rest went together to pay the remainder. In my opinion the government should compile a circular pertaining to the construction of the Shand dam, its cost, use and benefits, and send it to municipalities which suffer through the overflowing and flooding of other rivers, in the hope that, as an after-the-war work, they, too, may set up an authority much as the Grand river people have done to save themselves great losses. I heard the minister say this afternoon that the overflowing of some river in his province this spring set the community back about a million dollars. A million dollars would go a long way toward flood-proofing any ordinary river.

Would the minister give the
total cost of the Shand dam? While I am on my feet I may say that the Grand river is naturally flooding worse from year to year as the forest is disappearing; the snows disappear more quickly and the water runs out faster. I am not positive yet that the Shand dam is going to do all that the hon. member for Davenport claims for it. The flood was fairly serious this year. The dam has beeri completed for only a year or two, and as the hon. member suggested, it will, I believe, be a good thing if the government keep very close tab on what happens in that locality. The Grand river watershed is one of the most fertile places in Ontario. Will the minister state what is the total cost and what the receipts are to be from the Canadian Pacific Railway and other sources?

The cost of the scheme was estimated at $2,000,000, but the real cost is $2,051,516.49. Of that amount 37% per cent was paid by the Ontario government, or $715,000; 37% per cent by the dominion government, or the same amount, and 25 per cent by the municipalities, or $500,000.
The dam apparently cost $2,000,000, including easements.

Item agreed to.
Chief engineer's branch-Dredging- -Ontario-
509. Port Maitland-Repairs to west pier, $55,000.
I would remind the minister that this work is very necessary. The east pier is in equally bad shape.

This amount is to be expended as a result of the winter survey
Supply-Public Works

which was made there. We have a vote in the ordinary estimates, and this supplementary is to complete the work.

Item agreed to.
General-
512. War risk insurance-subject to allocation by the treasury board, $270,000.

Could we have some light on this item? My understanding of war risk insurance was that it was insurance the government was providing which private companies could not provide because they could not assume the risk. I should like to know what the amounts are comprising this $270,000, how they are placed and where, and any other information the minister has on the subject.

The $270,000 is to provide for payment of war risk insurance on properties under the jurisdiction of the department. These properties are valued1 at approximately $199,067,189 and are insurable for ninety per cent of the valuation, or $179,160,470. The premium is fifteen cents per $100, making a total of $268,740, or, in round figures, $270,000. The valuations are:
Harbour and river works	 $83,413,834
Public buildings outside Ottawa... 61.184,048
Public buildings at Ottawa	 47,559,409
Expropriated properties, Ottawa... 731,108 Furniture in rented quarters, Ottawa 1,211,103 Furniture in rented quarters outside
Ottawa	 2,362,927
Government telegraph branch property	 104,760
National Art gallery, works of art..	1,650,000
Canadian War memorial collection..	850,000
The issuance of this insurance was authorized by the War Risk Insurance Act, 1942, and by order in council P.C. 2/8917 of September 30, 1942.
If there is a loss under the war risk insurance, who pays that loss to the government?
I will admit I am not conversant with the act. The Minister of Finance put the bill through the house and, when his estimates are up, I have no doubt he will give the information.

But this is an item in the minister's estimates and I think he ought to have information on any item of his. It seems strange that the government should insure buildings and pay the insurance itself if there is a loss. Does the government carry ordinary insurance on its buildings?
No.
To whom is this $270,000 paid?
It comes back to the government. If the government puts insurance on one of its buildings and the building is destroyed, the government is the beneficiary.

But how can the government be the beneficiary when it must pay the loss incurred? If the government pays the insurance to itself, where does the benefit come in? I admit I may be dense about this, but I do not think I am the only one, judging from the information I have received.

I will call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the questions asked by the hon. member. I admit I have not made a study of the subject. I know an order in council was passed in 1942 and we are committed to the amount. I would not even say that it is a matter of bookkeeping, because I do not know. I would rather have the Minister of Finance give the explanation.
It is a strange situation. Here we have an item of $270,000, and not a minister can tell us why it is there or how it is to be explained.
My hon. friend should recall that war risk insurance covers not only public buildings, for which this premium provides, but a vast number of private buildings.
What does the minister mean by private buildings?
Whose private buildings?

Factories and warehouses in a city like Halifax, and private structures as against publicly-owned buildings. The premiums on all these properties are paid into a fund under the act, and what happens is this. If a government property is destroyed, the government collects the amount from the fund, and in that event the private owners who had taken out war risk insurance under the act would be paying a part of the loss in the premiums they paid.
Is the minister telling the committee that the government is putting war risk insurance on private property in Halifax?
No. The private owners pay it.

Then, if the private
owners pay, how is there an item in these estimates for it?

War risk insurance applies to nearly all private property in the country and the private owners pay premiums into the fund. The government

Supply-Public Works
also pays its premiums into the fund. If any damage occurs to a private property, the owners are paid compensation out of the fund, and if we suffer damages in our properties we receive from the common fund the amount of the damages incurred. That is the explanation.	[DOT]
This is the government premium for war risk insurance on government buildings?
Yes.
It is more than that.

Item agreed to.
Chief architect's branch-Special-
Construction, repairs and improvements-[DOT] Public buildings-
5IS. Toronto postal station "A"-Improvements (revote)-further amount required, $9,000.

I wish to say a few words on this item. My colleague here has been complaining that I have not said a word all day. I want to point out to the minister the deplorable conditions at the terminal "A" Toronto post office. We have no post office there except a part of the union station, which was to be only temporary, although the receipts are $9,000,000 a year. This policy of continually patching up the terminal "A" postal station is intolerable. The business men are complaining that they cannot get adequate service. The government erected a large post office building on the west side of Bay street and when the war started, they gave it to the ordnance corps. The ordnance corps should move out of this new postal unit, because the city gave the whole of the exhibition grounds to the army, and there are huts also of the Royal Canadian Air Force along the waterfront.
The time has come to stop this patching up in connection with the post office. The post office in Toronto is a public utility and modern conditions should prevail there. Does the government think the Bell Telephone or a gas company or the hydro could do business in a building such as terminal "A"? People cannot get the service to which they are entitled. There is a large volume of business carried on by the post office, and the platform and trucks are laden with postal matters, first-class, second-class and third-class mail. They simply need this new postal building. From the point of view of labour also, especially at Christmas time, the present state of affairs is intolerable. The last time his estimates were up the Postmaster General promised that the army would move out, but they have not done
so. Let the army move to the exhibition grounds. The post office cannot do business as it should and the result is that mail is delayed. It is a situation that can no longer be tolerated and I urge the minister to do something about it. Here we have $9,000 for temporary repairs or something of that sort, and in the main estimates $20,000, and last year, $72,000 for repairs to terminal "A." That sort of patching up cannot go on any longer. I ask the Minister of Public Works what he is going to do about the matter. Has he ever visited this property, to see the conditions that exist? Has he ever seen the conditions under which the mail is received and distributed in Toronto, as a result of which the people in the residential districts get only one delivery a day, while the business men down town are also all complaining? The staff and men are splendid. If you mail a letter in Ottawa on Thursday you will be lucky if it is delivered in Toronto on Monday.
The minister was able to construct two wharves at Burlington and another at Oakville, which are not used much except by a few yachts at the latter place, and surely, instead of this patchwork scheme, he could give the citizens of Toronto, who contribute over $9,000,000 in revenue, a little better postal building for service. There should be an order issued to the army to get out of this building, which is in the area of the harbour improvements. The time has come when they should move out. I pass there often and see a great many wagons and trucks going into that ordnance building, while the mail is all out on the platform at the depot. I ask the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General to look into the situation and have the army move out immediately, because the postal authorities, who render fine service, cannot handle the business properly in the fall of the year.

This is a rare
occasion, in that the Postmaster General and the hon. member for Broadview agree. I have received representations from the Postmaster General asking that the ordnance branch of the defence department clear out of the Toronto terminal and that the postal authorities be installed' there, so that we are advising national defence to erect another building or follow the suggestions made by the hon. member, and vacate the premises. We hope that in the near future the post office will occupy the whole of the building.

The minister is a lawyer,
and there should be an engineer at the head of the public works department. Eaton's or
Supply-Public Works

Simpson's would not tolerate that sort of thing. The minister has never visited the property, to see the conditions that exist. I do not believe any lawyer should ever be Minister of Public Works. Eaton's would not have a lawyer in charge of their construction work. A lawyer has to do with legal business, not with public works, and after all this a public utility and service should be the key. The conditions I have seen there at Christmas time are disgraceful, with eight or ten thousand employees handling mail. I ask the two ministers to try to clean up the situation before the fall.

Item agreed to.

515. To provide for claims and other expenses in connection with unemployment relief projects, $45,000.
I take it that these must be overdue accounts from some previous period, because I cannot quite conceive that in 1943 we. would want to appropriate any money for unemployment relief projects.
Shall the item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman.. I
am going to suggest that in spite of your desire for speed, at least the minister be given an opportunity to reply to my question.

This is a carryover. We had some dispute over the claims of two companies in Quebec who had the contract for the construction of the section of the Quebec intercepting sewer undertaken in 1939 as an unemployment relief project and completed in November, 1942. Ini full and final settlement the contractor Marcotte is to receive $32,098.25, and the contractor Auclair is to receive $12,901.72. When it came to settling the balances there was some difficulty. Now our engineers and their engineers have made a valuation and these are the amounts we believe should be paid.
There is no such project going on at the moment?
No; it is complete.
Item agreed to.
87. Departmental administration, $162,853.

I should like to say a word in regard to the request made by the hon. member for North Battleford that the minister take notice of the publication in the Toronto

Evening Telegram of an article by Max Eastman, which had been published previously in the Reader's Digest, and her suggestion that action be taken under the defence of Canada regulations. I am at a loss to understand how a request of this kind could be made logically by one who has been demanding in this house from time to time freedom of speech and freedom of the press. I just wish to say that there is no newspaper more loyal to the institutions of this country and to Canada as a whole than is the Evening Telegram, and I hope the minister will disregard the request of the hon. member for North Battleford.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I can only say that this article has been referred to the law officers of the department, whose experience in these matters has been long and varied. As yet I have not received any report from them. I am sure they will take note of the hon. member's testimonial to the loyalty of the Evening Telegram.

I hope the minister is not taking too seriously any suggestion that the law officers of the crown are likely to find anything unpatriotic or disloyal in regard to the Telegram. I suggest that the minister should not have been too serious when he spoke of referring the matter to the law officers, having in mind the situation as he knows it to exist.

I have been making some inquiries. I do not wish to make charges against any specific judge; but there have been cases such as the hon. member for Trinity cited when this matter was under debate in the house before,
where a judge had delayed judgment so long in a particular case that first of all the opposing counsel died before judgment was delivered; then the plaintiff passed away, then the defendant, and finally the judge died, the only one left in the case being the hon. member for Trinity who was acting as counsel for one side. Such cases are not frequent, I admit, throughout Canada, but there are just enough cases of prolonged reserved judgments to bring the judiciary in some parts of the country into disrepute. That is the reason for my rising.
A month or so ago a farmer came in to see me. He had heard that I had said something in the house about, reserved judgments, and he asked me, "Would you think thirteen years was long enough for a judge to make up his mind and give a judgment? I had a case that was tried in .1930, and while it was not a very important case it was important to me, but a judgment has not yet been handed down." I did think that thirteen years was a long period for the normal working of a judge's mind, and I bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice to prevent a scandalous situation from arising. To be frank, I think there is no excuse for a judge who is attempting to carry out his duties faithfully in war time to reserve judgment for an extraordinary length of time. The legal profession has a duty with respect to that, but lawyers generally are so anxious to please the judges that they do not press them too much. I am not interested in pleasing any judges in Canada; I think it is our duty in parliament to mention this matter, and then I am going to leave it with the minister to consider during the recess whether some check-up can be made in cases where there are inequities and injustices to litigants as a result of long delayed reserved judgments. Some kind of penalty should be imposed on judges who are not doing their duty in this respect. I am not so sure but that one penalty that would bring a recalcitrant judge to time would be this, that if a certain length of time had passed without judgment being given, the case be reheard and the costs on both sides and the court costs be borne personally by the judge. Something must be done to penalize the judge who does not discharge his duties within a reasonable time.
