Many of these are able-bodied men and women, but to-day they are not making the contribution they might make. It is in their interests that Hitler should be defeated and that the united nations should have the benefit of every ounce of energy that can be thrown into the conflict. I submit that if the recommendations of the royal commission had1 been acted upon, the penitentiaries of Canada would be organized to-day in such a way that the man-power now going to waste in those institutions might be devoted to some useful purpose. I should like the minister to make some comment with regard to the recommendations which were brought down by that commission.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: With respect to the report of the penitentiaries commission I must repeat what I said when the estimates were before the house last year. It will not be possible for me to take the responsibility of recommending the expenditure required to implement this report while this country is at war. The recommendations which do not involve large expenditures of money have been vey carefully considered, and most of them have been implemented to the degree to which that could be done without large expenditures of money. Again I have to come back to the British North America Act. Most of these high-minded gentlemen who talk about reforming the man who is so unfortunate as to be sentenced to some period of detention overlook the fact that ninety-five per cent of those condemned to detention are in no way under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice or any other federal department. They are serving sentences of less than twenty-four months in the common gaols, of which there are a great many throughout the country. The Department of Justice has no jurisdiction

over them other than to recommend to hia excellency, in appropriate cases, some degree of clemency. To carry out the social schemes or projects that are put forward by high-minded, public-spirited citizens would require a system under which the control of the gaols and penitentiaries would be under one authority. That does not exist and cannot be brought about under the British North America Act.

I am not satisfied with the explanation the minister has given. Would he be good enough to tell the committee how many people are in our penitentiaries now, and what provision is being made so that those confined in these institutions may make some useful contribution to the war effort?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The value of the
production, of penitentiary labour has more than doubled in the last two years, and a constant effort is being made to increase further the economic value of the work performed in the penitentiaries. All those who are connected with the administration of the penitentiaries realize, as I do, that merely employing the men so that their time passes must have a depressing moral effect upon those so employed, and it has been our constant endeavour to have them produce something which would give some tangible result for the manual labour performed. Prior to the war there was serious objection from labour unions and industry generally to allowing articles produced in the penitentiaries to come into competition with the products of free labour. Since the shortage of man-power has arisen, however, and since there has grown up such a large demand by departments of this government for various manufactured articles, we have found that without clashing with the labour unions or private industry we can make use of everything that can be produced in the penitentiaries.
As I say, there has been an increase of more than 100 per cent in the dollar value of the articles produced. In 1942-43 the value of the production of the penitentiaries, over and above that which was consumed in the institutions themselves, amounted to $382,008.20, of which $102,099.10 went into things we were able to do for the military forces. There has been a satisfactory decline in the population of the penitentiaries since the beginning of the war. At the present time that population is 2,980, while in 1938 the average was 3,618; in 1940, 3,736; 1940-41, 3,654; 1941-42, 3,380; 1942-43, 2,980, compared to a penitentiary and prison population of something like
75,000.

This penitentiary was established many years ago when coastal development was in its infancy. I believe the time is now opportune for a survey for a new location. Will the minister be good enough to undertake such a survey, having in mind the purpose of finding a new location, so that at the end of hostilities under, shall we say, a rehabilitation scheme, a new site may be developed. It is very easy at the present time to obtain 500 or 1,000 acres of land close to transportation facilities, areas which to my mind would be far more suitable for penitentiary purposes than the present site.
I have been given to understand that the city of New Westminster would be glad to enter into an arrangement with the penitentiaries authorities or the dominion government in connection with this land, because, if vacated by the penitentiary, it would make a valuable piece of residential property. A few days ago, when we were discussing certain estimates with respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, many members made some fine comments with respect to this famouns force. I shall not go over the things that were said then, but I wish to associate myself with those remarks. I am particularly concerned about one aspect of this item, the pay question. It is true that not long ago increases were authorized for certain ranks, and' I know these were appreciated, but we must also recognize the fact that, since these increases were granted, the rate of taxation has increased materially. I am of opinion that some of these men are in a more difficult position to-day than they were prior to the increase.
This matter was brought forcibly to my mind not long ago when a constable who has been with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for approximately twelve years showed me his pay cheque. The amount of the cheque was $82.50, with taxation deductions at the source of $30, leaving a cash income of $5250 for the month. I realize that certain allowances in the way of uniforms and billeting are made in the case of the single constable, but I wondered how we could expect a constable of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who is not permitted to engage in any other type of remunerative work, to carry on his duties when his net cash income for the month is only $52.50. We expect these men to be the personification of honesty, and I am not saying that they are not, but when you leave a constable with a net income of that amount you are developing a feeling in him that he would probably like to commit an infraction of the regulations and engage in some work during his spare time to supplement that $52.50.
The minister stated the other night that, while there is a ceiling on wages, we should not permit that to stand in the way when a situation such as this develops. When we consider the allowances granted to these men the salary may appear to be quite substantial, but we still cannot get around the fact that we are leaving them, members of the permanent force, single uniformed constables, with a cash

income of $52.50 a month. It is not proper, and I think further consideration should be given to this matter.

325. Naturalization branch, $64,460.

I should like to make a brief statement in connection with this item. When the war appropriation estimates of the Secretary of State were before the committee, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised the point as to whether a naturalized Canadian leaving Canada for the United States and taking his first papers in that country lost his Canadian citizenship. At the time I had not read the exact terms of the declaration of intention which he is required to take, but since then I have. He does not renounce his allegiance to the British crown. It simply says that as and when his final papers are granted he will. Consequently there is no loss of Canadian citizenship until the final papers are granted.

Would it be possible for
the minister to bring about a change in the requirements for naturalization with respect to the language qualification? It may seem strange to suggest that anyone who speaks neither English nor French should ask for a naturalization certificate, but a great many thousands of our people-I brought this to the attention of the Prime Minister on one occasion-came here from various countries of Europe twenty-five, thirty, forty or fifty years ago, and starting in as pioneers made Canada their home. That is particularly true of the western provinces. We have there people of Ukrainian, Polish, German and other origins. Wherever these people have settled in blocks it was impossible for them to learn the English language, because they never came into contact with the English-speaking people. Surely any pioneer who has lived here for twenty years or more and has a son or grandson in our armed forces in this war should be accepted as a citizen of this country and be granted a naturalization certificate if he applies. I receive tens of letters weekly

Supply-Trade and Commerce

from people in western Canada of various origins who have not had an opportunity to learn the English language and who were refused naturalization certificates when they applied, because of language qualification. Later, when they apply for old age pension- and some of them really need that assistance- they are refused it because they do not possess a naturalization certificate. I would appeal to the minister to consider this feature of the naturalization requirements with a view to bringing about some change, perhaps stipulating a knowledge of some other language, or some other requirement, so that these people who have settled as pioneers on the prairie provinces may be eligible for Canadian citizenship. I say that in all seriousness, because it seems unfair that these people who have devoted their lives in the upbuilding of this country should be refused naturalization certificates and, in consequence, some of them be refused the old age pension. I appeal to the minister to give this matter serious consideration.

I shall be very glad to
do so, but may I make a practical suggestion to the hon. member for Vegreville? As he knows, naturalization is one of the subjects considered by the committee on the defence of Canada regulations, which has not yet brought in its final report. It might be opportune for the hon. member to submit that matter to the committee for consideration at its next sitting.

I desire on this item to bring to the attention of the minister a number of, shall I say, complaints which have reached me from retail merchants, not only in Halifax city and throughout the province of Nova Scotia but in other portions of the maritimes. In peace time there would not be the criticism which I propose to offer, but on account of reduced staffs in retail stores, particularly so far as office help is concerned, merchants find it exceedingly difficult, not only to meet the requirements of this branch of the government, in compiling returns at the end of

each month, but to make the further returns which are required by the wartime prices and trade board at the end of each month, with respect to the amount of stock they have on hand, the sales they have made, and a large number of other items, which mean additional bookkeeping. More than one merchant has told me that it takes practically the entire time of one clerk or other member of his office staff to prepare the necessary returns which are required by three branches of government. I refer to the bureau of statistics, as regards returns for their particular records, the wartime prices and trade board at the end of each month, and the income tax office in connection with the same items, namely, the amount of stock which they have on hand at the beginning of the year, the quantity of purchases made for each month and for the entire twelve months, the gross profit, the estimated cost of the goods, and the net profit. All these items must be supplied by each and every individual making his return to the income tax office, and in addition he is obliged at the end of each month to make returns covering not all but a number of these items. Further than that, there is the monthly return to the dominion bureau of statistics with regard to trade matters.	,
Within the last two weeks the wartime prices and trade board sent out a form compelling merchants to give a survey of their business for the years 1939, 1940, 1941 and 1942, covering a large number of items. It is not so much the firms with up-to-date methods of bookkeeping as it is the large number of small merchants who are finding it exceedingly difficult to meet the requirements of these government bureaux in this respect. I could place on record the type of form which is required. Perhaps it is a good thing to have the statistics on file to advise merchants from month to month as to increases or decreases in the particular section of the country where they are doing business, in comparison with the rest of Canada. But I would point out that returns should be simplified in every way possible, and I base that contention largely on the fact that man-power at this time is extremely scarce, and that additional restrictions affecting retail staffs have recently been brought into effect by selective service. I ask the minister to give consideration to the elimination of at least two of these forms and the bringing of returns under one heading in as simplified a form as possible. Since I have already gone over some phases of this matter with the minister and some of his officials, I do not need to enlarge further upon it.

For instance, the monthly return-and this is every month-calls for the following information from every retailer: net sales, inventory of merchandise beginning the first of the period; merchandise purchased for the month or for that period; net cost of merchandise handled; inventory of merchandise at the end of the stated period; net cost of merchandise sold and gross trading profit.

speechtext: I can quite sympathize with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) because personally I have had practical experience in connection with the point he raises. 101. Combines Investigation Act, $30,250.

I am sorry to have to
discuss at this stage of the session the matter I have in hand, but so far there has been no other item under which I could bring it up earlier. It has to do with the effect of an alleged combine upon the employment of a gentleman in Toronto, Mr. Robert Stuart. On August 1 of last year, as reported at page 5176 of Hansard, I made reference to this matter. At that time I stated that this gentleman was an experienced salesman of electrical equipment; that he had been employed by several electrical companies one after the other, each of which had sought his services; but that in due course, owing, to what he alleges was a combination of these companies to control sales territories and sales, his services were dispensed with, and he alleges that the companies agreed not to reemploy him. On hearing the information I gave at that time, the minister said that the matter would be looked into and that, if the facts were found to be as claimed by Mr. Stuart, an investigation would be held. It appears that on August 18, 1942, Colonel the Hon. W. H. Price, exattorney general of Ontario, acting as solicitor for Mr. Robert Stuart, wrote the minister a letter which I feel I should read:
The Hon. Humphrey Mitchell,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Mitchell:
On August 1st, 1942, in the House of Commons when item 102 "Combines Investigation Act, $45,475," was going through committee, Mr. John R. MacNicol, M.P., brought to your attention a case of a gentleman, "R.S." I am attaching Hansard page 5176 which sets out what happened. The gentleman referred to was Robert Stuart, of 1 Brandon avenue, Toronto. Mr. Stuart has asked me to draft for him a declaration covering the facts of his case. I am enclosing that declaration, so that you will have it before you for consideration.
Mr. Stuart has been placed in a very bad position on account of the discrimination practised against him. He is a man now fifty years of age, and cannot get new types of employment readily. On a number of occasions he has made complaints to the companies involved, and I believe has brought the matter to the attention of the authorities. You will agree that a man like Mr. Stuart is not financially able to attack large companies who have discriminated against him. On that account the matter has dragged along without him getting any redress. Probably under these circumstances, with these facts before you, you will be able to investigate his case in such a way as not only to give him redress, but improve the situation which apparently still exists. He knows that he cannot get employment where
5346
Supply-Labour

he had it before, notwithstanding that he was successful as a salesman, and in great demand. There should be a remedy for a situation of this kind.
Enclosed with the letter was an affidavit which I shall not take time to read, since the Minister has a copy of it, giving the names of the various companies and setting out the various facts which Mr. Stuart claims to have information and affidavits to prove. I shall read just the last paragraph of this affidavit:
The above information has come to me from various sources in my capacity- as a salesman, and I now say that this combination of companies are a combine to fix prices and eliminate competition. In carrying out this plan they agreed not to employ me, and they did not employ me because it would interfere with their plans. I have suffered very greatly on this account, as these companies cover the whole range of my sales efforts. They are practically the only companies in Ontario from whom I can receive employment. I therefore request that the Department of Labour take such steps as -will enable me to obtain employment and at the same time put an end to the electrical ring.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath, and by virtue of The Canada Evidence Act.
To that letter and affidavit the minister replied, under date of September 9, 1942: Dear Colonel Price:
I have had careful inquiries made into the subject matter of your letter of August 18 and the declaration of Mr. Robert Stuart which you enclosed.
It appears that Mr. Stuart's submissions relate in the main to his past connections with certain electrical equipment companies. Remedy for the personal injury alleged would appear to be a matter of civil law. This, you will understand, is not a matter which can be considered under the Combines Investigation Act.
In addition, Mr. Stuart makes certain allegations with respect to the operations of certain companies engaged in the sale of transformers. The transactions which he describes are said to have occurred a number of years ago. The electrical supply industry is now subject to the control of the wartime prices and trade board, and the sale and supplying of transformers and related goods are, by order, under the direct supervision of the administrator of electrical apparatus and machinery. There does not appear to be ground for proceeding now with investigation under the Combines Investigation Act into these alleged transactions of a period in which the circumstances differed so greatly from those now prevailing.
I have a word to say in reference to that. I know this gentleman. He is a highly reputable and excellent citizen. The affidavit signed by him, and prepared by his legal adviser evidently reveals a situation in which he is barred from obtaining employment.

That, of course, is wholly and manifestly unfair, and, in my judgment, an infraction of the man's rights.
Investigations made recently in the United States before a senate committee reveal that a large number of companies in that country have been carrying on under a combination. The lines covered by those various combinations include companies manufacturing magnesium metal, and materials made from it, zinc, rubber, gasoline, electrical equipment, plastics, dye stuffs, tungsten, carbide and some others. The one to which I am referring particularly is electrical equipment.
After a most exhaustive investigation into these various combines, the assistant attorney general for the United States appeared before the senate committee and made this statement:
Mr. Arnold: I appear before this committee to present a bill to correct those pressing patent abuses which have so disastrously affected our war effort. Through these abuses * a vital segment of American economy has been strait-jacketed into a foreign cartel system, and the free flow of strategic materials vital for war and for internal security has been impeded and delayed.
This committee has a peculiar responsibility -it has investigated the patent system at a time when it was never more important that we have full and unhampered production and that American business be entirely free of either old or prospective commitments to cartels.
The assistant attorney general asked1 for prohibition of combines of that kind. I am asking the minister again to read carefully Colonel Price's letter of August 18, and Mr. Stuart's affidavit which came with it. If the minister has not a copy, I shall send him this one. I would ask him then to read his own reply. Then I would suggest that he send an investigator to Toronto, to see Mr. Robert Stuart, and obtain from him proof of his statements in the affidavit. If the minister's investigator finds that those charges are substantiated, then I suggest that the minister have some action taken to see that this man gets fair play. He is entitled to it, as a British citizen.
Hon, HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour): I shall be glad to do that.

There is one matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I should have liked to have more opportunity to go into it more comprehensively, but perhaps my purpose will be served if I leave with the minister the suggestion that he go into the matter and see if something cannot be

Supply-Labour
done to rectify what would seem to be a grievance held by Montreal aircraft lodge No. 712 of the international association of machinists. The minister will recognize the situation I describe. It has to do with three Montreal aircraft companies, namely, Vickers, Fairchild and Noorduyn. This is a union which represents a large number of employees in those three aircraft plants. During last year and into this spring the whole matter of the levelling out of wage scale in the aircraft industry in Montreal and in other areas has been under consideration. This union is one which can be recognized as a good example of an association of employees which is trying to play ball with the men they represent, with the government and with the public. That is no reflection upon other unions, because, after all, I think that, if one takes them by and large, he will find that the labour unions of Canada are prepared to play ball, not only1 just as well as other sections of our country but in some cases, if I may say so, just a little better. I believe in this particular instance the minister will realize at once what the officers of this union had to go through until this spring, when their case finally was heard by the new national war labour board.
It was not an easy thing to avert some action by employees in these plants, but they did hold off a strike, or other precipitate action, on the understanding that their waiting until the decision was given by the national war labour board would not be prejudicial to their case. However, in bringing down its decision, the national war labour board was unable, under the terms of the reference, or on account of its jurisdiction,, to make an award which could operate retroactively. This placed the union and its officials in a difficult position, and one which those belonging to the union find it difficult to understand.
At the same time it seemed unfair to my mind to penalize the union by virtue of the fact that retroactivity was not possible under the ruling of the national war labour board. I do not intend this evening to enter into any lengthy discussion, but I wish only to leave with the minister the suggestion that he investigate this situation and, if possible, make the award retroactive to the time negotiations were commenced, or when the complaint was first laid.
The minister may say that he cannot do that, in view of existing legislation. I would ask him to review the situation with respect to the legislation, and if he finds it is impossible to do anything with existing machinery, to consider seriously the question of providing machinery by which a remedy could be
effected. I shall leave this matter with the minister for his consideration. I should have liked to discuss it in greater detail, but the lateness of the session, and of the hour, does not permit my entering into any lengthy discourse on the merits of the case. I should like the minister to undertake an investigation of this and to see if some remedy and perhaps some restoration cannot be brought about.

I have been in close touch with this organization in Montreal, namely, lodge No. 712. I came in contact with it when I was chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission, and I think the union itself will admit that we made a distinct contribution to the working of that organization in Montreal. It must be remembered that they are not a low-paid category.
They are not paid the existing rates in a similar industry.
Their rates are as high as the railway rates.

They are not paid as
high as those paid by Canadian Car and Foundry.

They are, but I am not arguing that point. I appreciate my hon. friend's interest in this matter. The national war labour board, under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice McTague, were generous in the adjudication of this dispute. A request was made officially to me for an amending order which would permit the establishment of the maximum bonus in the aeroplane industry in Montreal. The total amount to be payable over a twelve month period was estimated to be $7,500,000. When I was chairman of the national war labour board I felt that that board should recommend and adjudicate on matters of wages brought before it by labour organizations and employers. I think myself it would be unwise-my hon. friend will understand-for the government to interfere in the affairs of the board which in my judgment are rendering a distinct service to the working people and employers of this country.
The minister must have heard me wrongly; I suggested no such thing.
I understood that.

I understand that the decision of the war labour board was that it should only go that far; that the legislation under which it operated prevented it from going any farther.

If I gathered aright the meaning of the minister's words, the government has passed a set of regulations under which the board is unable to do what it should do with respect to this dispute. The board, under the government's regulations, goes as far as it can, and the government feels it should not interfere in the decision of the board. That seems to me to be establishing a most astonishing situation. That is the sort of thing which indicates insincerity with the men, and I think something should be done about it. I am not satisfied with the minister's explanation.

I do not wish to enter into any extended discussion on this matter, but I believe that the treatment which has been accorded to our labouring men who have acted in good faith will not be conducive to happy relations between the government and labour. This is a serious matter.
Mr. MaoNICOL: Earlier in the session I expressed sympathy for the hard-working Minister of Labour in the multiplicity of troubles he has to unravel. At that time I said that I wished I could do something to help him. Since then, I have given this matter a good deal of thought and I am going to make a suggestion. Everyone knows that industrial peace is most desirable in peace time, and certainly it is most desirable in time of war. I have always been one who believed that labour should receive a fair return; that the conditions under which labour worked should be of the highest. On the other hand, I have always advocated that the employer should also receive fair consideration. At the present time we are having a number of industrial disputes. We have the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and the industrial disputes inquiry commission to defend the interests of labour. In times of peace these have given good satisfaction, but the question now is whether their procedure is speedy enough. I have always felt, in all my dealings with men, that we should follow the biblical phrase:
Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him.
I have always thought that the quicker an industrial dispute could be settled, the better, and I question whether the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and the industrial disputes inquiry commission can give rapid enough action. I was wondering if the minister or

the governor in council would consider the appointment of one or more royal commissioners. These would need to be men with many years of legal experience in labour disputes. There are lawyers in this country who have spent many years in studying and adjusting labour problems, men who have come up from the ranks and who have equipped themselves with a thorough knowledge of labour. I would suggest that such a man should be a lawyer with at least ten years' experience at the bar in order that he be steadied down and have some stability and knowledge of how to deal with labouring men and companies from experience when there is friction between the two. I am going to ask the minister to consider this matter, because I believe this would offer means of settling industrial disputes immediately. The industrial disputes royal commissioner could be sent from his own department; he would be a permanent official, and could assist in settling the dispute immediately. It is imperative that the least possible amount of labour be lost through disputes.

I am fairly well acquainted with the background of these disputes, because I went over them quite recently. I did not raise the matter to-night, because I did not think it would be proper under the item we are discussing. As a matter of fact, I do not think it properly comes under the estimates that are before us to-night, except possibly that a question of this kind might be considered under Department of Labour administration. However, I am not going to continue the debate, except to say that it has been a habit with the Department of Labour to continue over a long period the adjudication of industrial disputes. I could mention half a dozen or more disputes that went on for months and probably years but since the national war labour board was set up there has been considerable improvement. In this particular case, however, I believe that an injustice has been done and that some means should be provided whereby such injustices could be rectified. I do not think it is a matter that the minister can do himself. It would only lead to endless trouble if the minister undertook to interfere and make decisions on his own. The proper procedure for the department, if the machinery is not working properly, is to set up machinery that will work properly, and the minister would act only when the matter was brought to his attention either in or out of the house. I am satisfied that these workers should have received their settlement to a date farther back than was set.

Supply-Labour

Could the minister assure the committee that the problems of which the labouring people concerned complain in a pamphlet called "Crisis in Steel" prepared by C. H. Millard, have been taken care of so that they are on their way to being cleared up? I have read the pamphlet with considerable care, and although I do not wish to go into the matter at this late stage, I believe that it is the duty of this committee to have an assurance from the minister that the difficulties discussed in the pamphlet are being cleared up.
Before the minister makes any reply, I might point out that this is one of the problems which I had in mind when I said some time ago that I feared this house was going to leave its duties and go home before it had done the things it should do here. I think the hon. member for Davenport spoke wisely when he spoke of the danger of creating friction between the government and labour at this time. We seem to be succeeding very well in the war, but let us never forget for a moment that we can lose this war and lose it disastrously if we provoke labouring men in this country to action which they might justifiably consider they were entitled to take in their own self-defence.
I do not believe the government has played square with labour in the past year. I believe the government has been insincere; I believe it has betrayed labour in more cases than one. I am just going to ask the minister now if he can assure the committee that the matters complained of in this pamphlet are being looked after and that a solution of the problem is honestly and earnestly and sincerely being sought.

I assure my hon. friend that the matter is being looked into and that it is being honestly and earnestly and sincerely looked into. I have read the pamphlet he speaks of and have also had conferences with the organization concerned, but I think my hon. friend will agree with me that while this is a perfectly free forum, it is not always the best place to settle industrial disputes. If my hon. friends are ever fortunate enough or unfortunate enough to lead a ministry in this country and my hon. friend becomes Minister of Labour, I am sure he will appreciate that the difficulties and complexities of industrial disputes vary greatly; they do not run in one pattern.
I do not wish to take up further time of the committee, so that I will say just briefly that the organization we are continually developing for the settling of industrial disputes has developed, I think every unbiased observer
will agree, to a stage where it can hardly be compared with the organization we had three years ago. After all is said and done the national war labour board and the regional boards are experimental in character and like all human institutions they are not perfect. But many of the people who criticize the instruments we are using at the moment I feel sure, when the war is over, will be the very ones who will demand their retention because now there is a place for labour to go to where there was not one before. We have dealt with over 16,000 applications with respect to wages and bonus in the past year through our regional and national war labour boards.
My hon. friend may rest assured that the conference I had with the steel workers was a satisfactory one and that steps are being taken by their organization to make the necessary representations to the national war labour board with respect to their claims. But I do not think it serves any good purpose in the cause of settling industrial disputes to suggest insincerity. I do not think that is good for the country. I believe that the record of this country in handling labour disputes in comparison with others of the united nations reflects credit upon Canada in a big way. There are some exceptions, of course; but, generally speaking, I believe that it reflects credit not only upon the employees but upon the employers of this country. In 1917, when we had a much smaller industrial structure than we have to-day, there were two and a half times as many labour disputes. In 1937, in peace time, there were more man hours lost than there were last year. While labour disputes always make the newspaper headlines, very little is said of the day by day work of the conciliation service of the Department of Labour working in conjunction with the respective provincial departments in ironing out industrial disputes in this precarious and difficult time.

I appreciate the minister's frankness and also his statement that the House of Commons is probably not the best place to settle labour disputes. But I think the minister will grant that it is the inescapable duty of any responsible member of parliament, when he sees abuses or what he deems to be abuses to bring them before the high court of parliament.
Certainly.
And I am quite sure that the minister will grant that I am only discharging what I deem to be my duty as a member of parliament.

There are a few words I wish to say on the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, with particular reference to men coming out of the army. It is not working out as I, at least, thought it would. Until a few days ago I was of opinion that the contribution of the man who served in the armed forces was paid by the government, and that when he came back and went into an insurable employment, if he met with unemployment, he was covered by the act. I find that I was wrong in that assumption, and I have two specific cases with which to support that statement.
In a little booklet put out by the unemployment insurance administration from their office, it says, in section 7, with reference to men serving in the armed forces, that any period spent in the armed forces since July 1, 1941, will count for benefit, ''if you establish that you had within one year from discharge ninety days of insurable employment." That is the joker. The two cases to which I refer are those of two men who were discharged from the army, came back, and went into employment in two coal mines which had a disaster. They were not out of the army and employed long enough to work the ninety days called for by the act, having been thrown out of employment by something which was, of course, unforeseen; nevertheless their claim is held up, and while the ordinary employee of these collieries immediately after the accident happened came under the Unemployment Insurance Act for benefit, the two ex-servicemen, by virtue of that particular clause, did not. Their claims went to the board of referees, and they teceived a decision from the board that because they had not had ninety days in insurable employment they did not qualify for benefit. I bring that to the minister's attention, because it is something which will have to be ironed out. I see a lot of trouble ahead for men in the forces who may run into that kind of situation on account of not having had sufficient time in an insurable employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: How long had they worked?

Less than ninety days. One had worked, I believe, thirty days, and the other a little less.
There is something else in connection with theUnemployment Insurance Act which I should like to leave with the minister. I am merely going to provoke his thoughts on these two 
some of the offices in action. I think they are doing a good job with the staffs they have. These offices were originally set up to carry the unemployment insurance business, and they have inherited the job of selective service; in addition to that, many of them are carrying on the welfare work as applied) to men discharged from the army. They are bearing a load which they are not staffed to carry, and steps should be taken to see that these offices are adequately staffed. My observation in going into many of them-and I have been in quite a few, because I do not miss a chance at checking up on them, because I visualize the machinery now set up as permanent machinery which will play an important part in rehabilitation after the war-leads me to think that many of them are being set up on the assumption that they are functioning simply for war purposes. I consider that is wrong. That may not be the intention of the minister or his deputy, but the whole thing seems to be operating on that basis. These offices should be adequately staffed.
Second, many of the men who are carrying that load in the offices and working a sixteen-hour day, although they have been employed there for the past two years and in some cases two and a half years, are still temporary, em-points. I refer now to the offices. I have seen ployees as far as the civil service is concerned. It is not a pleasant position for the man who is handling a job of this kind, taking a lot of responsibility, and certainly not receiving wages commensurate with the responsibility of the job, to be also in an insecure position, practically waiting for someone to replace him. Many of the men to whom I have talked take the attitude, '' It looks to me as though I am just doing the job while it is rough and tough, on the temporary payroll, and that as soon as the war is over, the returned men will get the preference and the chances are I shall be bumped into the street." That is not a satisfactory position for a man who is doing an important job and laying down important machinery. These men should be appointed permanent employees; they should1 at least be given the protection which affords them some stability, so that they will know where they stand and where they will be within the next few years. Also I think the staff should be increased. There are many complaints, but as far as the offices I have been in are concerned I do not hold the personnel responsible. There are not enough employees. In the matter of the welfare officers the Minister of Pensions and National Health, I suggest, should push his department to see that in every important

Supply-Labour-Unemployment Insurance
unemployment insurance centre a welfare officer is installed. There is quite a load involved in the rehabilitation end. So that the three matters which I should like the minister to check up on are: first, the feature of unemployment insurance which militates against the ex-serviceman, so that the system does not work out as it was intended to; second, permanency of employment for men engaged in the unemployment insurance offices; third, in adequate staff in these offices, so that the system will be built up permanently.

I thank my hon. friend for bringing these matters to my attention. As a matter of fact, his first suggestion is news to me, and will doubtless be of interest to the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I have already had discussions on the question of staff. I was in one of the largest cities in Canada the other day, where 20,000 men pass through the offices in a week-almost a division and a half. I said to the regional director, "Supposing you had to deal with 50,000 men, as you might have to do if the war should end to-morrow, or suddenly." I am trying to take the long view of it, that, whatever government is in power in this country at the conclusion of the war, in my judgment there will be set in motion social services of a kind and character which I believe all hon. members think should be instituted in this dominion, and what we are endeavouring to do is to build a machine which will take that load.
What my hon. friend says about the hard work which is being undertaken by these local employees of the selective service is true. It is also true of the headquarters staff. I sometimes wonder how they have been able to maintain it without a break-down in the last twelve months. A tremendous load has been placed on this organization, and when all is said and done it is a question of organization. What I hope we shall get out of this is a trained corps of experts to deal with the problems of the working men and women of this country. Of course that will take time.
As regards the question of permanency, that, of course, is governed by a general policy in all departments. No permanent officials are appointed to the civil service during the war period.
On the question of salaries, I can assure my hon. friend that I do not regard this as my fault; that I have pressed the civil service commission and other agencies of government charged with that responsibility, in an effort to build up what I consider a proper basis of remuneration for people working in this department. I should like to pay them tribute.
I know that to wear the soldier's uniform is a glorious thing, but let us remember that numbers of these people are working sixteen hours nearly every day in the week so as to get this machinery which we have set in motion in the best possible working order. I hope that when the war is over, whoever is Minister of Labour will have an organization which will be prepared to take the load of what I consider necessary social insurance when this time rolls around.

May I make one suggestion to the Minister of Labour regarding the unemployment insurance offices? Canada is becoming a great industrial organization; the workers are moving onward to that better day, and as one who has examined some of the offices, might I say that I find, regarding the men appointed to many of the offices, too much stress has been placed on office experience as a prerequisite of appointment? I say this- and I say it in no disparaging sense-that if the minister himself were not Minister of Labour, he might find it difficult to obtain a position in one of the unemployment insurance offices, because, when his application was submitted, they would look at the office experience he had had. I suggest that in this country we are drifting to the same state that exists in Great Britain where there is a caste system. Not long ago the civil service in this city thought the educational qualifications of the men were a little too low and so they brought in some men with M.A. and B.A. after their names; but if you look around the city and ask where those men are, you will find that many of them are the biggest duds that ever were appointed. I am not against education. Far from it; the race from which I have sprung has always laid emphasis on the importance of education. But I am more for the practical man, and you will find that in the British House of Commons this very question was discussed not long ago. It may startle many hon. members to know what a labour man in the House of Commons there had to say on this question. Let me quote:
"As a result of the inefficient and undemocratic system now prevailing", Brown said, "the chance of a boy of 'inferior education' of getting to the top grades in our public service are literally non-existent. A man's educational 'marks' follow him through his career and it is very fortunate that the Prime Minister did not get into the service. His educational qualifications would have kept him in obscurity all his life."
Mr. Churchill, who was educated at Harrow, one of England's best schools, was "a bad student" and his "educational qualifications very low", Brown declared, adding: "Take Lord Beaverbrook. Like Churchill he could not have

passed better than a clerical examination. Yet he is, obviously, a man of amazing drive and capacity and even had he got into the civil service he would have been chucked out."
I have visited many offices and know men who have received appointments, and I can say that many of them have never worked in a factory in their lives. They may be qualified in other ways, but'I do not think they are qualified to talk to practical men such as coal miners and mechanics. The Prime Minister has taken an interest in labour men in this country, and I urge upon him that it is not necessary that men should have long lists of degrees before they can obtain positions in any of these offices. What is important is that men with greater practical experience, who have sympathy with the men that come before them, should be appointed. I do not mean, of course, that the men in the offices have no sympathy, but I emphasize the importance of that point. The Minister of Labour is a true labour man, and he has an opportunity to see that more practical men from the factories are given positions in these offices.

The two examples brought forward by the hon. member for Cape Breton South bring to my mind a great many thoughts in regard to returned men. I wonder if the Minister of Pensions and National Health would tell the committee whether or not precautions are taken as rapidly as possible to see that such injustices to returned men are rendered impossible. It seems to me that to make returned men ineligible for the benefits of unemployment insurance because they were in the king's uniform instead of being in the ranks of labour is nothing but a blot on our whole way of doing things. Could we have some word from the minister of pensions or the Minister of Labour in this regard? I am astonished that we should have allowed to develop in the country a set of circumstances under which men are discriminated against as were the two to whom the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred. Can the minister of pensions tell the committee what precautions are taken to ensure that this does not happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I shall be glad to discuss that in detail tomorrow when my estimates are up.

With respect to the unemployment insurance vote, as I understand it, the offices of the unemployment insurance organization form the nucleus for the national selective service. I endorse at least that part cf the speech which I heard of the hon.
'Mr. Eeid.]
member for New Westminster. I was just coming into the chamber as he was progressing with his argument. One of the grave difficulties; one of the great complaints that come to me and other hon. members of the house, is with regard to the quality of the personnel, in some instances, chosen by the government in connection with national selective service and unemployment insurance work. It is not fair to make a blanket criticism of all local offices of the organization, but it is important to bear this in mind. If ever there were a place where people of the right type were required to handle work of this description, it is in the offices of the unemployment insurance or the national selective service, because I am convinced that either success or failure depends largely upon the relations that are created between, on the one hand, employer or employee and, on the other hand, the general public. Too much care cannot be exercised by the government in the choice of these men. One fault I find with the government is that all this matter of national selective service, coupled as it is with unemployment insurance offices, started far too late as far as the war effort is concerned. One of the difficulties that the minister now has is to find the right men. Men are not as easy to find as they were at one time. As the hon. member for New Westminster will readily admit, the minister is having difficulty in getting the right type of men for the local offices and the general organization. It is not sufficient for the minister to say that he is having a good deal of trouble on that score because the government's policy, framed as it was, has made it impossible to get the men who normally should have been got at an earlier stage.
I simply rose to endorse the principles laid down by the hon. member for New Westminster. The complaint that is made is that too often the wrong people are attempting to carry on this work throughout Canada. It has been one of the blots on the whole situation in connection with these offices throughout the dominion. Returns have been brought down which show, if one reads between the lines, the difficulty which the minister is having, and it is a difficulty which he need not blame upon misfortune or chance, because the government of which he is a member must, in my opinion, take responsibility for the fact that the work was started far too late and that too little was done in the earlier stages in connection with both national selective service and the organization of these offices which have to do with that end of the work.

Supply-Labour-Unemployment Insurance
I conclude my remarks by saying to the minister that there is much to be desired with regard to the whole question of local offices as far as these organizations go.

I thank the hon. member for New Westminster for the suggestion he has made. There is a great deal to be said in favour of it. I agree with him, and in the last six or seven months we have been taking greater cognizance of the aspect of the problem which he has mentioned.
May I say to the leader of the opposition that unfortunately many of the men we should like to get are in the armed services, and the government cannot be blamed for that.
I do blame the government in this way, that national selective service started too late. That is the root of the whole trouble.

I have made some study of unemployment insurance in Great Britain for many years. I do not say that in any boastful way. When they started in Britain they took in only seven or eight trades. We established our unemployment insurance system in 1941, and I think it was the best and biggest organization job ever done in this country. I believe it will compare favourably with what has been done in any country in the world, in the speed with which the organization was set up and in the way in which it has functioned; I think that statement will meet the approval of impartial observers anywhere. Of course we started on a much larger scale, in conformity with the size of the country, than they did in Britain.
Let me say this, as I have said in other places. People are not fence posts or bottles of milk. You cannot push them around; they are human beings. While engineers and people of that kind have done magnificent things in a material sense, the engineering of men and women is a much more difficult problem than the engineering of material things. As I said earlier, what we hope to get out of this on the whole is an organization of what I might call experts in the engineering of men and women, because, after all, it is only chance that the fellow who is on this side of the desk in an unemployment insurance office is not on the other side of the desk, asking for a job. I think I can say that in the long run we have to sell service to the people of Canada, who are responsible for the creation of this organization.

I, too, believe that the hon. member for New Westminster did well to bring this matter to the attention of the committee. I have had the feeling also that altogether too much attention has been paid to academic qualifications and certain rules and regulations, and not nearly enough to the stuff of which the individual concerned is made. I should like to commend the minister if he is causing more attention to be paid the human element, and not so much to the question of educational qualifications.

Since we are working overtime, and there is no pay for it, there is no reason why I should not get into this discussion, though I am not going to take very much time. I agree with the minister that the unemployment insurance commission has done a difficult job at least fairly well. In anything I have had to do with the commission, in anything I have taken up with the chairman, the difficulty has been straightened out very quickly, and infinite pains have been taken in doing so. I think we must agree, however, that to find people not only with academic training but with training in dealing with men and women is not an easy task, and we are not going to get those men and women any more easily by reducing the educational qualifications. What we need is not less but more education; then we shall have more people from whom to choose. These difficulties will remain until the people as a whole have acquired a social way of looking at these matters. I only rose to say that in the short time the commission has been functioning and in the abnormal circumstances which have prevailed, I believe a very good job has been done.
